LADIES' LETTERS
MT DEAR NELLIE.

I am an admirer of artistic hair-dressing. I may inform you that the revived style of dressing the hair at the back, instead of on the top of the head, necessitates even more elaborate waving than did the high coiffure, and most women have learned by sad experience that it simply ruins their own hair to have it waved even two or three times in the course of the week; but with transformations now sold for the purpose, all such trouble is avoided, and the length of time occupied by one's toilette shortened in a quite wonderful manner.

-a clothing is the subjem _ ..erable thought in this severe weather. It is not always realised that to keep the extreanities mistily clad is a most important point. Woollen -stockings and thick boots would save the necessity for an extra wrar, and would be free from the disad- vantage of causing a sudden chill, -as the wrap often does when discarded. In the same way, warm underclothing is far from more to the pur- pose than thick outdoor clothes, which are often so heavy as to impede the limbs in taking the necessary eremite.

Imptemptu fancy dress parties are a fancy of the moment, and create a good deal of amusement at country house parties. Orders go forth in the afternoon that everyone is to appear at the dinner with heads dressed to represent any character they please—or the whole table may elect to repre- sent well-known characters from famous painters. One recently personated the beautiful Mary Duchess of Rutland, after Sir Joshua Reynolds; hair combed off the forehead, piled high on top, twisted in and out with gauze ribbons, crowned by three nodding ostrich feathers, and two love curls drooping on to the neck behind. Another repre- senting Lady Hamilton wore a broad, shady straw int, trimmed with loops of brown ribbon, and tied across the crown, holding the brim down on either wide, with a white scarf the hair floats loose on the shoulders. The St. James's and the St. Giles's -Beauties, after Bartolezzisvelllknown engravings, are splendid heads to copy, the St. James's beauty having a much-becurlect fair wig, with lace lappets and pink ribbons at the back of the head, a fillet of blue ribbon round the top of the hair, nodding white plumes placed well at the back, a string of .pearls encircling the fringe, and a white gauze scarf brought from the top of the hair and passed softly r.eact the throat.

There is a noticeable tendency towards the use of very stiff rich brocades for ceremonious dresses -to be worn at night, brocades interwoven with gold thread and patterned with blurred flowers of the mellowest shades. A bodice and train of such a sabric looks sumptuous over a silk muslin petti- coat, one mass of flounces and lace insertions, the bodice deeply pointed in front, hut with the usual harsh line of the Court corsage draped with a sash which must have flat ends, of brocade lined with sprigged or plain satin. All the newest ,sashes are fist and stiff, like bell-pulls, and very arnate with their fringed ends and quaint em• broideries. I saw a lovely black velvet hat, which, on a tall, stylish woman, would have looked charming. It was trimmed with yellow lace and black ostrich plumes, and had a very fascinating up-turned curve at the side, which revealed the wavy tresses of hair beauif ally dressed in the latest style. The lace made a pretty, soft trimming against the lace, where it fell over the curved brim. A Louis XV. hat in Nile green felt was trimmed with pink roses and velvet-leaves, the leaves decorating one aide of the hat underneath the brim and falling down at the back with pretty, graceful effect. Folds of Nile green panne velvet trimmed the crown of the hat.

Ruffles and boas are more and more in demand now the weather has set in colder, but I think the wear of them makes the throat delicate and sus- ceptible to colas. The prettiest I have seen were of cut tulle or chiffon, and smartest of all are the ostrich feather ones. For the winter fur ones are the correct thing, and make a pretty present. A fancy of the moment is the wearing of a bunch of' natural violets pinned in the hat, or half hidden in the crilpe bow of a mourning hat or bonnet. These violets are only worn by those in deuil in this way, although many women adopt a favourite flower as their badge, generally some of the sweet- scented ones.
Your Living JENNIE.

Canada has received a large order for khaki clothing from the War Office. Fowls with tails IS feet long have been bred in an interior province of China. Parisian gourmets last winter consumed nearly 800 tons of snails. Herr Krupp has presented the pension fund of the Essen Steel Foundry with a New Year's gift of £25,000.
MOTOR MAIL SERVICE BETWEEN LiVERPOOL AND MANCHESTER.

As we previously announced a contract has bum entered into between the Post Office and the Man- chester Haulage Company for tha conveyance of the night mail from Manchester to Liverpool and from Liverpool to Manchester by means of the company's motore. This is another indication of the march of the timer. A number of motors are already employed by the Pelt Office, Lut only between London and piaess within a reasonable distance from it, such as Guildford. This contract is the first experiment of the kiad in the provinces, and will consequently be watched with con- siderable interest.

It is about eight years since the Post Office,discarding the railway, instituted a night mail coach service be- tween Liverpool and Manchester. Its inauguration was for some days a local topic, and the departure of the first coach, or, so to epeak more ccrrectly. a van, was witnessed ty thousands of people. A guard accom- panied the driver, and both were armed with revolvers. Since then the service has been maintained admirably. After the first few days the departure of the night mail only excited • passing interest, and since then it has attracted no attention at all. Happily through all the years which have since elapsed no unfortunate in eident has occurred to disturb the hum-drum re- gularity of the service. An attack on the night mail would have snacle fine re t ding, tut an affair of that sort it is hoped, will never occur.

Now' another change is impending. Horses sup- planted the railway, and they are to be displaced by the motor. The conveyances stipulated for will not be!tke light, swift cars which are favoured by the aristocrats and plutocrats of the country, but business-like vehicles capable of carrying a ton and a half. The journey will be accomplished in shot tt.r time than is new taken,and there will be a gain in that respect. On the question of cost the Post Office must have been satisfied before deciding upon the experiment. It was not until severe tests had been made that this decision was arrived at. The two points which most impressed those who wit nessed the trials were the ease with which an engine- driven vehicle can climb a hill, atd the absolute control the driver has over it, even when going at a high rate of speed. A motor going at twenty miles an hour was stcpped in the same distance that would be required in the case of a horsed vehit le travelling at seven miles an Lour. The change frcm horses to motors will be made in the spring.

aavertisoment, wn:cn, t ANt,neve, eutnnates frm you." And he took up a slip from his pocket, and read it slowly through. It ran thus : "To South American explorers and travellers. Wanted to find the rightful owner of a curious old Gold Idol, believed to have been discovered in British Guiana by a party of travellers about four years ago. Owner can , have it on giving correct description and adducing proper evidence in support of claim. Addrese, 4.e." "That is my advertisement," said the Doctor. " Doyou claim the Gold Idol ?" Does it belong to you?" "I don't know whether it is the one I know oi, or whether or not I can call myself the rightful owner," was the reply. "But lam one of a party who found an idol of gold in British Guiana four years ago—and I wish with all my heart I had never seen it. If it is the one I mean, it has curious golden hair." The Doctor nodded. '

" Ah ! Well, the other two—my friends—are both dead, so I suppose it belongs to me now. I was to have had a third share of whatever we might obtain for it, and we expected the British Museum would give a large sum for it. But now—the very ides of taking money for it turns me sick." Dr. L— raised his eyebrows. "It is very curious," he said slowly, " but that's the very feeling the man expresses who now has the image. I put that advertisement in, in the hope that some one would claim it and relieve him of its cus- tody." This time it was Neldon who nodded his head.

"I thought as much," he observed quietly. "Well, for myself, my sole object is simply to prevent its doing further mischief—creating greater misery. If I get it back I shall just take it out to sea and drop it overboard." For nearly a minute Dr. L— regarded him in silence. Then he spoke again gravely. "There is some strange mystery in all this," be said, "which I confess myself utterly unable to un- ravel. But I have seen enough to know that by some means, mischief—a malady that baffles me—is being spread. Somehow, everyone brought in con- tact with that gold image falls a victim to a mys- terious illness that I cannot diagnose. The man who has had it in his possession for the past four years is lying.ill at the hospital at which I am the Consult- ing Physician -; not only, that, there axe other cases, and they seem to be on the increase." . . . .
- The 'speaker uttered these last words with hesi- tation, as though making the admission with reluc- tance. Then he went on :

" You must know that at this hospital—a large institution at the East End, near the docks—we have frequently very strange and puzzlingcases. We get patients from all parts of the world ; fereigners from the east, from the west, from every known clime. And at times they bring their own particular dis- eases with them. I have met with many obscure and mystifying maladies unknown to English phy- sicians. Sometimes—generally—l have succeeded in discovering the proper treatment; but this is the most embarrassing of them all, and what makes it se serious is that it is spreading. It seems almost as though a new form of plague had been introduce Us. Can you throw any light upon it? If the idol, or whatever it is were of any other material, I should conclude thitt it carries with it the contagious germ of some disease unknown to modern science. Bat that theory is not tenable here, for how can a metal such as gold convey contagion ? The C 3131• plaint does not seem fatal ; no one has yet died of it, so far as I am aware ; it is a wasting sickness that wrecks the cDnstitution of the strongest, and sets up what seems to be a lingering process of de- cay.".

i'deldon shuddered. " I know," he murmured, "look at me." "You, too. are a victim to the same thing then? I thought so the moment I set my eyes on you." " Yes. But it has gone on longer in me than in the others you have seen, I fancy. . _

"The symptoms point to blood poisoning of a new description. Possibly it affects some constitutions differently from others. I wonder how it will affect me? For I know that I also have contracted it." And when lfeldon uttered an exclamation of sur- prise, the Doctor added, " Yes, it is so, my friend, we are both in the same boat, I fear." . _ _ _

" In my belief that golden image carries a curse with it," 3leldon answered with emphasis. "Let me do as I suggest, drop it into the sea. Then the curse may cease to work—at least it will not enfold fresh victims."'

Dr. L-- looked sceptical. "That sounds like mere illogical superstition, my dear sir," he said with a superior air. We scien- tific men don't believe in that kind of thing, you know. We believe that there is a natural cause for everything—if we can but find it." "Let me tell you what occurred to us," was Meldon's answer. "Then you will see that I have reason for my belief, even if it is, as you say, super- stitious."

div.head: GOLD IDOL,
div.p: THE GOLD IDOL,
FRANK AUBREY , (Author of" The Decil7Tree of El Dorado,' ft.)
/ - PART I. -CHANTER I.

England's colony in South America,' British Guiana is a countiy that, since the time of Sir Walter Raleigh, has ever teemed with mystery and suggestions of romance. And it remains to-dry very much what it was then, as regards possible dis- coveries, a region of fascinating potentialities. Though much has been accomplished of late years in the way of exploration yet vast tracts of its forest land are still utterly unknown. There are mountains, too, which, being surrounded by belts of primeval forest so dense as to be practically impenetrable, have never yet been ascended; and about these, as well, as about the nntraversed forests, the Indians have many curious tales to tell, tales of strange; unknown peoples and ancient cities said to be still existing there. And these stories derive additional interest from the fact that travellers have stated that at night they have seen on these mountains lights for which they could not in any way account • and this statement has been made by European explorers and scientists, whose credibility cannot be impeached. It was in the vicinity 9f one of these unexplored mountains—near that undefined borderland between British Guiana and Venezuela whichrecently threat- ened to involve us in a dispute with the United States—that a party of travellers, some years ago, made a curious and unexpected discovery. The party consisted of three Englishmen and a few native In- dians, the former being, respectively, Dr. Elder- field, a veteran explorer and antiquarian; Mr. Allan Feudal, a botanist; and a friend of the latter, Ar- thur Meldon' a young man of good family, who had joined the expedition out of pure love of adventure. The mountain near which they were encamped is called by the Indians Maleema, and they found it to be surrounded by a belt or zone of forest of such dense growth as to baffle all their efforts to penetrate it beyond a comparatively short distance -from the edge. But the place teemed with new and wonder- ful, flowers, orchids and other rare plants the like of which they had never seen before, and this fact Leaded to console them for their failure to penetrate to the mountain itself, and for the dangers, fatigues, and privations they had undergone in their journey to the place. And these had been by no means of a light and trivial character. Food of all kinds was scarce, the sole inhabitants being a few tribes of Indians, and these only to be met with in certain dis- tricts. Extensive tracts of the country are wild solitudes, given over entirely to nature in its most savage form, and the strange animals, birds, reptiles and insects which flourish beneath the tropical sun. Here one may travel—as travellers have actually re- corded—as many as thirty days together, without the sight of a human being, other than those in the traveller's own party; and naturally, therefore, supplies of food must be included in the expedition, and, when they run short, a fresh stock is difficult to procure..

Eendal and Elderfield's party were in difficulty as to food, so much so that it was threatening to bring their attempted exploration of this mountain to an abrupt conclusion. Of tinned provisions, flour, and some other necessaries—for themselves—they had a fairly good supply, and fresh meat could be had by hunting. The difficulty was that the ea:team—upon which the Indians almost exclusively subsist—was running short; thus they would soon be with Out food for their native guides and carriers. Then a council was held and it was decided to send their chief guide Malao, and another Indian, on a visit to an Indian village, said to exist about two days' jour. nay distant, and called Lennamouta, with a view to treating for supplies of the all-ixnporant cassava. To this Malao had strongly objected, declaring that the people at this village were reputed to be savage and unfriendly, jealous of all who ventured upon their territory, and fiercely vindictive. But, in the end, his scruples had been overruled, and he had ,been Prevailed upon to start. It was during his absence that the discovery to which I have referred was made.

Elderfield and Pemba, wandering farther afield than usual around the fringe of the forest belt, came, greatly to their surprise, upon a sort of path or track running into the wood, and so clearly de fined, that it had obviously been much used, and that recently. They returned to the camp for their friend, and then all three set out to explore this most unexpected :nystery. The track led them far into the depths of the sombre forest, with its giant trees and tangled undergrowth of gigantic creepers, until they came to an extensive clearing filled with the most extraor- dinary, most fantastic ruins and sculptures they had ever seen or thought of. Remains of temples, pal- aces and other edifices, all of solid stone, were to be seen on every side scattered about in wild confusion; but beyond, and occupying a large clearing by it- self, was a ring formed of a collection of huge rocks sculptured with remarkable skill into the likeness of all kinds of men, women, animals and birds. It was, in fact, as Elderfield aptly expressed it, "a sort of glorified Stonehenge; " and the strange mystery of its presence in that gloomy forest rooted the three travellers to the spot. They stood speechless, gaz- ing at the spectacle with awe and wonder. Atone end waS what seemed to be an altar. It consisted of a urge stone block of curious shape; originally, ap- parently, it had been in the form of a star, with grooves sunk into the stone that led to overhanging spouts like the lips of a jug. Elderfield at once divined and pointed out their object.

"They were to drain off the -blood of the victims sacrificed upon this altar," he explained, "that it might be caught in vessels placed under these spouts." "Do you suppose the victims were human be- ings I." neked Meldon with a shudder. _ .

" I should say yes, almost beyond a doubt," re- plied the antiquary. In the course of investigations carried on during the next day or two, the travellers discovered a vault beneath the altar, containing stone coffins and many strange articles of ancient workmanship. There were several vessels and ornaments of gold, and fixed on a stone slab, similar to that outside, but Analler, was a small image or idol, about twelve inehes high, of solid gold, with a pedestal of the same metal. he image was of skilful workman- ip, but not &ore so than much that has before lx-en-met with in ancient graves supposed to be those of the Incas, or perhaps, of some still more ancient race that flourished on the South American Condi- ent untold ages ago. But this Gold Idol had ono peculiarity of a most extraordinary character—it had gollen hair hanging from its head. This hair seemed to be of fine threads of pure gold, and was very soft and glossy. Dr. Elderfield pronounced it to be unique. "Never have I seen or heard of any- tl lug like it," he declared..

emu-ran IT. Dr. L—, the well-known London specialist, was seated in his consulting room in his house in Harley Street, to all appearance occupied in looking through some papers before him, but in reality lis- tening for the advent of an expected visitor. From time to time he consulted his watch, rose, and paced the room impatiently ; then he would sit down again and endeavour to interest himself in some qf the various written sheets that strewed his table. Once he talked to himself :

" I wish he would come," thus ran his words. "This affair is getting serious. And, when he does, let us hope he may be the right man, and may be able to throw some light upon it. I confess Ido not see my way how to act, or what more I can do." Then there came a knock at the front door, fol- lowed by a ring at the " visitor's " bell, and half a minute later the expected visitor was ushered in. It was Arthur Meldon. But he was a very differ- ent person fr)m the light-hearted, high-spirited young fellow, whose bold. adventurous spirit had carried him four years before through arduous ex- plorations under tropical suns, through perils and escapes by land and sea; whose dauntless courage had faced death a dozen times when threatened by sav- age beasts, and still more savage men. Now he looked broken dowlk and almost decrepit. His tall figure was bowed, and in his eyes there was a lack-lustre, weary, hopeless expression that was almost piteous to see. Above all, the pallor of his face was un- natural, ghastly. It was as thcrugh he wore a mask of dough, tlrrough which his eyes but feebly glim- mered. Dr. L— almost started at the sight of him ; even in the long experience of the celebrated physician he had never seen a face like this. "You are Mr. Arthur Meklon ?" he began. And. when the visitor bowed acquiescence, added, Pray be a?ated, sir. rather u.xpected to see—"

"I understand," the other answered wearily, when the doctor hesitated. "You expected to see a very different person—a younger looking man. Yet, sir, I am only thirty-three; and I know I look sixty !" The physician started slightly again, then cross. lug the room, he went up to his visitor and peered seachingly into his face. Returning-to his seat, he said curtly "I see—the same symptoms." "I expect so; I am not surprised to hear you say so," Meldon answered. "However, I have not come about myself. as von are aware, but about_this

div.head: CIIAPTEII
div.p: CIIAPTEII
Moldon told the physician tho history of the find- ing of the idol, as already given hero, and then went on :

" So far our expedition had ,been in every way successful, but, from the time we brought that ac- cursed image into our camp we never knew a dav free from trouble, or danger, or accident or—dea4. The next day Malao the guide came back with serious news. The people he had gone to see weie furious at our ' invasion ' of their country, as they phrased it, and threatened all sort of things. They would come and drive us away in a few days, they said, and, even if we went away before they came, they would send the ‘.Kaleema ' after us."

61Kaleema !" exclaimed Dr. L—. "Why that's the word Collins—the one who brought the image to this country—raves about. 'What does it mean f" " Kalecma ' means secret poisoner.' When an Indian—or a tribe—declares a deadly feud against an enemy, he engages the services of a 6 Kaleema.' This man—so the Indians state—follows up the in- tended victim secretly, ruthlessly, relentlessly. Sooner or later, in some disguise, he is sure to come up with him, and take him in an unguarded moment. They have various methods of carrying out their purpose ; have all sorts of subtle poisons ; indeed, they are the most expert people going in compound- ing, and the most skilful in administering their dead- ly preparations to their victims. Their poisons are of various kinds; they do not, as a rule, kill at once, but inflict some lasting, lingering injury. Sometimes a leg or an arm will gradually decay and drop of! ; sometimes the victim loses his eyesight ; sometimes he lingers on and wastes slowly, as in my case ; sometimes the malady is intermittent. It takes the form of a deadly sickness, which yet does not kill ; goes away of itself, only to return, with regularity, once a year, so that the wretched victim has it al- ways hanging over him, and is yet deluded in the' intervals—at first—with the hope that he is cured. This was the case with me—at firet ; and it is so still to some extent. Twice a year I fall into a fear- ful illness, and get better again ; but each time it leaves worse traces behind."
" Ah," said the Doctor, " that is the case with Collins and the others."

"Yes, I expected as muchi. You see the idea of these fiendish poisoners is not to kill, but to torture —and for long years. To kill at once is too slight a punishment to satisfy their notions of revenge. They aim at renderlng the sufferer's life a misery to him for as many years as possible. Even in hunting, when they use poisoned darts and arrows, they em- ploy a preparation that only suspends animation and does not actually destroy life. They shoot at an animal, and if they hit it, it falls drrwn stupefied-- not dead. I have seen it many times. They can do the same, they say, with human beings." " Horrible ! I can scarcely credit it !" " Ah, but it is so, and in administering these various forms of poison to human enemies, the-' Kai- eema ' goes to work with the same end in view. He does not give it in food or drink, which might be difficult in the case of one on his guard ; he merely pricks the skin with a poisoned needle—probably when the victim is asleep. The prick is so slight that it is scarcely felt, or the doomed man fancies an ant has stung him, and only turns over and goes to sleep awpain, if he is waked up. ell, soch is the horror and fear that these men inspire, that the mere threat of thain will always terrorise your ordinary Indian, to whatever tribe he may belong. So, when the Indians at Lennamouta threatened to send the Kaleema ' after us, our natives were seized with ungovernable panic. It had already been arranged that we should break up into two parties for the return journey, Dr. Elder- field wishing to travel back to the coast through Venezuela, and Mr. Fendal to make the journey through Guiana, the route by which we had come. I went with the latter, and I was the only one who returned alive. Elderfield died on the way down— of fever it was said ; and my poor friend Ferulalex- pired in my arms, of fever also, it was thought, but poisoned, as I feel convinced; though how or when, or by whom, I never could find out." "But why? What had you done ?" " Oh ! it seems that the tribe we had offended still carried on some idolatrous worship at the place at which we found the Golden Idol. Twice a year they met there and held a grand festival, accom- panied with human sacrifices. They went to the place just after we had left, and soon found we had removed the idol, and .they then pursued us. We had confided the accursed thing to Eldertiekl, or I think WC' ahniiki have trivpn it on Mail a n.irtv

tEe tribe came up with i us, after a few shots, wliich did no one any -harm had been exchanged, they asked for a parley, and begged us to give up their sacred god.' We assured them we had not got it. They even offered us gold dust—and plenty of it— for it. They seemed Co be rich, those people. Event- ually they went away, pretending to be friendly, but in reality, as I feel convinced, :nitructing their ‘Kaleema 'to keep on our trail. Hi, no doubt, was one of the natives ' we afterwards fell in with, as we thought, by accident, and joined our party os- tensibly as a carrier, but really to • carry out his treacherous errand, and steal back the sacred god' if he could get hold of it." The Doctor drew a long, deep breath. "I see. A nice pickle to be in truly: And you never heard what became of the precious image ?' - "No, only that Elderfield just lived to fall in with anarty who had net out from the cotist to meet him. Ileard that through an Indian; but who they were, or what became of the idol, I never knew. I have but just returned to England, and have not yet been able to interview any of Elderfielcl's friends or rela- tives. But when I saw your advertisement I guessed that it referred to the same Gold Idol, and a convic- tion forced itself upon me- that it was still creating mischief, else why should its present holder be so anxious to find the rightful' one? It must be worth £l,OOO for its weight of gold alone." / "But after all that you have said," observed the Doctor, "we seem no nearer daylight." "I fear it is so," answered Melclon. " But what account does this man Collins give of his possession of the image ?" t "Merely that it was confided to his care by a man on board a vessel in which both *ere sailors. The man was taken ill and died suddenly. He had been up country—Venezuela, I believe—and had returned, bringing this image and some other curiosities with him. He said they were not his own; but that he had undertaken to deliver them to an address in Eng- land that Collins would find amongst some papers in his chest. Collins hunted through it, but could find no directions, so he had to keep the articles. But he declares that it has worried him ever since that he ()mild not deliver them to the rightful owner, and the foolish fellow has got it into his head that this strange illness is a kind of punishment in conse- quence. And he thinks he will never get well till he has discharged his trust." _ .
"It is all very strange. Is he poor ?" "Yes, very."
"He 'must be an honest fellow."

"Ha is. He showed the image to me soon after he left the hospital the first time. He had already talked to me about it, and I felt great interest in the affair. I pointed out that, being so poor, he would be quite Instilled; in all the circumstances, in sel- ling it. But he would not listen to it. I even offered to find him a purchaser, and borrowed it to show to cwo or three I thought likely buyers. Strange to say, they are all now patients on my hands, with symptoms similar to his. Would you like to see Collins and question him yourself F" " I should, very much. "Can you come now? lam going there myself, and you can accompany me, if you like." This was agreed to, and the two started for the hospital together.
(To be Continued)

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Scme idea of the immense size of Buckingham Palau. may be gathered irom the fact that there are over 250 clocks in different rooms throughout the building, and that it is more than one person's work to keep them all going. Some of thew are very old and antique, and very curious in their design, but none are allowed to fall out of order or become useless. There are some that date back to the time of Louis XlV,and many are valu- able works of art. George 111 had a weakness for col- lecting old and curious clocks, and there is one at Buckingham Palace which tells the height of the barometer each day, the state of the moon and tides,the hours of sunrise and sunset, the day of the week, the inoath of the year. and gives otkr informing details. Great interest has been taken in the new stamps, King Edward being the first British Sovereign whose accession has neeessitated a change of design. When Queen 'Victoria came to the throne, there were no adhe- sive stamps, the penny postage cot being introduced until May 1839- 'The first penny stamps were black, being afterwards changed to red, the brick red variety being issued up to the year 1881, when our recent form of stamps came into vogue.Tbe unused red pcony stamps issued up to twenty-one years ago, are said to be now worth several 'shillings each amongst collectors' and many people will no doubt keep a numLer of those bear- ing our late Queen's effigy, ard of which no more will be issued. Just now our letter boxes are everyday stuffed full of handbills' circulars and atalogues of business houses, Tbe New Year tieing the usual time chosen for extra pushing and advertising. A bachelor who writes to one of the London papers on the subj,ct rays it is a pity that business firms do not discriminate a little,as he has no use for feeding bottles, articles of feminine attire,and so on. At the same time he expresses surprise that there should be no such thing as sales at men's hosiers, tailors, and so on, Whilst pretty nearly every estab- lishment patronised ty wemen is in the midst of the New Year sales, one never sees or hears of such things at men's establishments, and it would certainly seem that Mr_ Bachelor has some cause for complaint on this score.

The season on the Riviera will somewhat suffer from the early meeting of Parliament, and the forthcominz Coronation will also tend to keep visitors away. " The King,who,much to the discemeture of the Court gossips has a habit of keeping his liana to himself, is expected to go to the Mediterranean in March, when Queen Alexandra will he sway on a visit to her father, the King of Denmark. Lord Salisbur3,, accompanied by his daughter. Lady Gsvendoline Cecil, will also spend part of the spring abroad, and Lord Rosehery will shortly go as usual, to his place at Naples. The ex-Premier wid have Lady Sybil Primrose with hire, and he will ilso entertain Lord and Lady Crewe during his stay abroad. Lady Hely-Hutchinson utters a word of warning against the emigration of untrained and incompetent women to South Africa. According to the wife of the Governor ef Cape Colony, most of the women going out belong to one of two dosser. Firstly there are the dainty lady helps, pretentious, delicate, and incanahlt,. Secondly those who are flighty, common-minded, pur- poseless, ignorant, lazy, and inefficient. Lady Hutchin- son blames the emigration Societies for sending out many undesirables, there are enough of these already in South Africa. The women that are wanted in that country are those capab'e of deal;ng with the busineis side jot things, whether in teaching, or other duties, and all should have a knowledge of household work, home dressmaking, cooking, laundry work, and small farm ing. Lady Warwick has instituted such a course of training for won3enfat her hostel at Reading, but our best women colonists are of course those who have gained their knowledge and experience in their own home life.

There are those who think that we shall one day find relief from the everlasting meal-getting by obtaining ready cooked dinners from the distributing kitcher. ' When cooks will cease from worrying, and servants tyrannise no more. Others believe that before long we shall obtain our meals from the chemists in the form of concentrated tabloids, and there are already, both in Paris and New York, restaurants where the three or four tabloid meal may be had. But neither theory is likely to be matured in our time. It is true that many in order to avoid trouble with servants, or personal household ties, are taking to living in fiats, and obtain- ing their supplies from one central cooking department. Many wools now give their dinner parties at the hotels or restaurants, and find them infinitely less trouble, and co more ,xpensive than giving them at home. Still the great majority of women would be lost for occupation witty ut the kitchen, nor is it desirable that it should be abolished.

How best to conceal the—to many women—all necessary powder-puff, when travelling, shopping, or paying calls, is a problem difficult of solw.:iou. Pockets are forbidden, and there is seldom sufficient room in the little tags that hang from the waist or wrist for even the Emallcst epee- men. Some women fasten a morsel of se ansdown to , the centre of a dainty lace handkerchief, and stuff this up a sleeve, but the latest idea, which hails from Paris, is a better one still. Few would guess that the dair ty buttonhole ad sweetly-smelling violets, surrounded by the most natural looking green leaves, is ir reality a I puff, and which reveals itself when the little silken ribbon which holds the stalks is loosened. Yet such is the case, and this dainty trifle should be secured by all to whom the powder-puff is a necessity. In the old days of tucks perpendicular and horizantal, few could have dreamed of the height to which the art is now csrried. Both skirts and bodices are frequently fitted to the wearers by the skilful way in which the material is nipped up between finger and thumb. and , run in the most infinitisimal of tucks, row upon row. This is a delightful mode for winter and spring, as it adds ernativ to the warmth as well as the strength and durability of a gown. Speaking of warmth, there are many charming materials to be had, which will be eagerly welcomed by the delicate among us. For example there are cotter - faced fabrics, with warm woollen backs which mks splendid morning blouses, and there are delicate !olkieg silks with cosy woollen hacks for evening wear. How grateful girls Phould be for these. A decade ago,if thsy had delicate chests they had to wear woollen materials at dames when everyone else was in silk Or chiffon. Now fragile member s of the community may trip it with the best of them, and who shall say if their gowns are silk all through or not. Although the year of Court mourning has almost come to an end, a great number of black and white gowns are in course of preparation for coming festivL ties. Few combinations are more becoming to the average woman, and none in better taste. For quiet wear, the black sstin evening skirt is in considerable request, sometimes in its plain- simplicity, at others with an overskirt of chiffon, lace or net, to match the blouse. Sequirs are extensively utilised despite all that has been said to the contrary. They render brie ht and attractive many a black gown that would otherwise be distinctly dowdy. MA DOE.

div.p: DOES IT MATTER TO YOU, OR ME

Down by the wood when day is done, Does " Somebody" wancPring o To watch the gleam of the waning sec, Or the purple afterglow ? And if he look long in the /eafy lane Under an old oak tree, Where " Someone " perchance might ccam again —Dces it matter to you, or me ? Down by the lane when stars shine out, Does " Someone " coyly creep, First glancing timidly round at:wilt, Then—under an oak tree peep? A glint ty the trees, now near, now far, If she's not surprised to see— A " VVill-o'-thr-wisp or a red cigar —Does it matter to you, or me? Down by the wood, 'neath moonbeams clear, If two young folks should meet, If " Somebody " whispers in " Someone's " ear A secret sweet, co sweet. If two hearts dream a dream so fair Where nobedy's near to see, If " Somebody'i lips meet, " Sornene's " there —Does it matter to you, or MR ? div.head: WORKMEN AND FRIENDLY
div.p: WORKMEN AND FRIENDLY
SOCIETIES.
An Astonishing Ancoats Case.

If it were not for the friendly societies and trades unions many workmen would be in a perplexing plight when overtaken by illness, and without their customary wages. These organisations have helped many a hard- working man over a difficult time, when, without their help, they would likely financially go under. There 13 very little disposition on the part of the members to take advantage of the sick benefit clauses, and it is only when absolutely compelled to lay up that they do so. In fact, there are instances on record where members have applied to be written off the benefit list before it was advisable that they should. There is the case of Junes Henry Farrow, a stock-keeper in a Manchester warehouse, 37 yeara of age, the details of which he told to a reporter at his clean, cosy, well-furnished home, at Lind-street, Holt Town, Ancoats. The reporter had been made acquainted with the out- lines of Mr Farrow's case, in Elolt Town, and had called upon him to bear his story from hiS own lips. "I have teen a member of the'Order of Druids," he said, and in 1889 my firatoickness started. It was rheumatism ia

Nield, Manchester.) the back,and I had it close on six months. I consulted a doctor four times, and being a member of the Omer of Druids I was allowed sick pay. This is a diminishing weekly amount, according to the time you are HI on the book!. At the beginning of 1890, I did not want to be on the books of the Order any longer. It had got to half-a-crown pr week, so I asked the doctor to sign me off. He told me I wasn't fit for work, but he did what I asked him. A friend bad advised me to have a vapour bath once a es esk, and for five weeks I took his advice at some baths in Itochdale-road. At first I felt much better, hut after the fourth bath my appetite went, and after the fifth my back got worse. I suffered terrible pain. Then somebody told me to apply fomentations, which I did, but still suffered great pain. In a short time my ribs became bad, and I nad curvature of the spine." "That was bad? " "It was bad, I can assure you. I went back to tha doctor again and told him what! had been doing. He said Whoever recommended you that treatment might have sent you to your grave. Go home, ard lay on your back until you are told to get up.' For more than six months I lay on my back in bed." " Did the doctor attend you all that time ?" " He did, and I took two bottles of medicine per week. I was then induced to cossult another doctor, who told me I would be better in the Royal Infirmary than at home. I could just walk. I went into the Infirmary, where I was placed in a jacket of plaster of Paris. Then they sent me to the Convalescent Home at Southport, bet I got worse instead of better, and went back to the Manchester Infirmary. Then I was at borne for six months unable to do anything. At the end of that period I was re-admitted to the Infirmary. That was in 1891. I began to lose the use of my hips, and I thought the jacket was too tight and stopped the circul- ation of the blood, but I continued to wear it. For over eighteen weeks I was in bed, simply resting. I was getting sick and weary of the confinement. I was very weak as you may imagine, and when I got out of bed I could scarcely crawl ; but they sent me to the Convalescent Hospital at Cheadle. I had to be carried there into and from the hopital vas. Instead of getting better I got worse, The electric battery was applied to me at various times during the eighteen weeks I was at Cheadle. The doctors could twist my legs into all sorts of shapes by electricity, but I could not feel the shocks I longed to walk, and requested to be allowed to try. Up to that time I had always been wheeled about the grounds in a chair, I found that by taking held of the arms of the chair, which ran on castors, if I kept my legs straight, I could get a few yards, but only let my legs get a bit bent and down I went. One day I dragged myself by the aid of a chair to divine service in the chapel, but the agony I suffered was horrible, and I was carried back to bed. In May, 1891, I asked for my Ws— barge. They had done their utmost for me, and I felt that I was incurable. A week Cr two before I asked for my discharge the doctors stuck needles into my legs and thighs, but I had no feelleg.e " Did they let you go ? " Yes, they plac.d me in a hammock. I was 9'15- pendeci in it in the omnibus to the Infirmary at M cnester. and then I got home somehow in a cab, cut of which they had to carry me into the haual." " What was the neat thing you trial ?" "One day in Rey, my Ls:either William, who lives its Newton Heath, said to me " I have heard se much, and have read so much, of Dr Williams' pink pills for pa'e people, and knowing a chap who was cured of dropsy by teeiing them, that if you will try them I will pay for them.' " " And you accepted his offer ?" " I did. I took two boxes, but was no better. My brother kept urging me toga on with them, and I did so, carefully following the instructions sent with the pills, and after the fourth box I was cured and able to resume my employment." " And had you no recurrence of the Meese ?" " Yes; lot me tell ye.e. For two years I kept to my work, and then I was taken bad again, but instead of taking Dr Williams' pink pills, as I ought to have done, I went to the Convalescent Home in Seuthport, haying great faith in the place. That was in 1595." " And hew.did you g, t on there ?' " I am sorry to say I did not get better, and the doctor said I bad better go home. I came home, but I couldn't walk. They had to carry me to bed. 1 tried various things people recommended to me. One thing I tried was a gill of porter every night, but that proved a failure. We were getting very poor, and I may tell you that one night we had neither money nor food in the house. The landlord of a beerhouse in this street came to see me. He stood near where you are sitting, and he gave me 2s. With that 24 I determined to give Dr Williams' pink pills another trial. I sent to Boots, cash chemists, in Oldham-street, and begin again. I took four boxes, one after the other, but was no better. My brother kept calling upon me and urged nie to per- severe. I did so, following the instruction, to the letter. I got a fifth, and before I had finished ICI got a little strength in my legs. I took other two boxes getting stronger every day. Before the eighth box was finished I was able to go to my employment. " And have you been at work over since P " " I eave, and I am stronger and heartier than ever. You should see me eat."

And he sprang to his feet with alacrity and showed me his hands and arms, and waxed loud in his praiee3 of Dr Williams' pink pills. Bringing his fist down on the table to emphasize his words, he said : " I don't know what to say to you or how to express my thank- fulness for what Dr Williams' pink pills have done for me. div.p: VOLUNTEER INTELLIGENCE.

F. and G. Companies 2nd V.B.C.R. Detachment orders by Captain G F Ashton, for week endiag January llth, 1902. 1. The drills for trainea Volunteers will commence on Friday evesing, the 10th inst., at 7 30. Recruits every Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday at 7.45. 2. Conditions of efficiency.—The tollowing Soecial Army Order, dated War Office, 24th December, 1901, is published for information : (1) The attention of the Volunteer Force is directed to Section 7 of " Vclunteer Regulations respecting the conditions of efficiency for officers and volunteers," issued with Army Order 246 of 1901, viz.: "In exceptional cases which may arise in any year, where it can be shown that a corps has made 'every effort to fulfil the requirements of efficiency, as luid down in the Order in Council of 4th November, 1901, but has wholly, or as regards some of its members, failed to de so, the general officer commanding will be informed of the facts, and any application recommended by him for exemption from the conditionstwill receive the special consideration of the Secretary of State.".

(2) This section is intended to meet the special Cade of an officer appointed, or Volunteer enrolled, previous to the date of issue of the above Army Order, and who, during the period of his present engagement with the corps, may be able to satisfy hiajcommanding cfficer that owing to his civil occuriation, he is prevented wholly or partially from attending camp in any year. Such; engagement will not be' held to extend beyond let November 1904. (3) Similarly, in the event of a corps satisfying the Commander-in-Chief, On the special recommendation of he general officer commanding that, in consequence of ,its having experienced exceptional difficulties, it is prt- .vented from complying with the prescribed conditions Its case will be specially considered. (4) Volunteers of all ranks should, however, under- stand that in viow ef recent developments in the con- ditions and requirements of modern warfare, the training of troops, regular or auxiliary, must be con- ducted on a systematic and progressive principle, in which practice in the essential duties ot war is an imperative feature. (5) For some years past the Vulunteer Farce has con- stantly claimed to be seriously accepted as a reliable and organized section of the Army for home defence. It is now determined that the responsibility claimed shall be roallzed. Under thiyold regulations it was impossible for either an officer or Voluntner, although he might become technically efficient so as to earn grants for his corpq, to attain the high standard of efficiency now requisite to enable him to take his appointed place in the military organization and defence of the kingdom. (6) It follows that the force must adopt itself to such a system of training as will admit of its members, from the highest to the lowest, ,being exercised and inspected in actual tactical operations over suitable country, or in the actual works of defence. An annual camp, with which the year's training should in this manner culminate, is therefore indispensable. To tacilitate suoti training in the case of those corps which, in the opinion of the G.0.C., are unable to train in complete units, provisional regiments, or battalions under officers of the regular troops, and con- sisting of batteries or companies.datailed from Volunteer 1 Corps, will be formed at suitable stations during certain months of the camping season. Further instruc- tions regarding these arrangements will be issued in '1 due course.

(7) It is fully realized that the civil occupation of. some Voluuteers will not admit of their complying wlth the minimum conditions necessary for an effective course of milhary training, and that consequently the force must ultimately lose the services of such men. It is preferable to have a somew hat smaller number of more highly trained officers and men sufficient to meet all the demands for home defence• - -

(8) The State requires that a suitable standard of military training shall be secured in return for the out- lay of money, end consequently the enrolment in future of officers and Volunteers who are unable to afford adequate time for any military training beyond elemen- tary barrack square ;drill cannot be permitted. (9) While it is confidently expected that officers and Volunteers will endeavonr to meet the changes necessi- tated by the development of modern warfare, the opera- tion of the regulal ions will be carefully watched, and any atnendments which experience shows are desirable will be effected.
••• (10) A copy of Mil Army Order to be inserted in the regimental orders of every Volunteer Corps. By order, (Signed) G. F. ASHTON, Captain Commanding Detachment. Runeorr. Jan. 6, 1902.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
LATCHFORD V. FRODSHAM.

Played at Latchford on rather a heavy ground. Prom the start the home team had the best of the game, and event- ually ran out winners by four goals to nil. Grounds was very conspicuous in the forwards, scoring on three OCERBiOI3B, Banks securing the fourth. Dixon. at half back, also played a good game, whilst for the visitors. Jenkins, in goal, was in fine form, saving several excellent shots. The full tacks also played a good defensive same. LATCHFORD " A" V. SALE "13."

At Sale on Saturday, and one of the most enjoyable games of the season, terminated in a win for Sale " B "by rive goals to Latchford "A " two goals. The goals were sacred by I+l Cliffe for Latchford, whilst W Knight played a 1:no game. The defence of the backs and goal-keeper prevented a much larger core being run up.
MACCLFCEIFIELD V. STJEKTON HEATH.

Played at Stockton Heath on Saturday. Both teams were strongly reptesentenl. Ten minutes from the stArt Maccles- field opened the scoring, and Brough added another just before half time though the point waS certainly offside. Within five minutes from time the home team scored their Only goal, and a hard and fast game resulted Macclesfield, two goals; Stockton Heath, one.

div.p: WARRINGTON ,TOWN COUNCIL. The Appointment of Tramways Manager.

A rneeting of the Warrington Town Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. In the absence of the Mayor, the chair was occupied by the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman H. Roberts). There were also present :—Aldermen Sutton, Monks, Shaw Green, Francomb, Fairclough, Bolton, Hutchinson Councillors Plumpton, Malkin, Brough, F R Roberts. William Roberts, Sampson, Ellison, James Evans, S Davies, Baird, Burton, A Jolley, L Greening, Forshaw, Duncan, Bennet, Tinnion, John Evans, John Roberto, Wilkinson, William Pierpoint, Hulse, A J Jolley, Pea- cocke, Shillcock. Rogers, witu Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), S Wilson (deputy town clerk), J Fairhurst, (borough treasurer), W S Haddock (gas engineer), and W H Grimsdale (electrical engineer)

div.head: INDISPOSITION OF Tn
div.p: INDISPOSITION OF Tn

The TOWN CLERK Intimated that the Mayor was absent owing to indisposition. On the motion of Alderman SUTTON, seconded by Alderman FAIRCLOI7OII. Alderman Roberts, as Deputy- Mayor was voted to the chair.

_ The DEPIITY-MAYOR said he was glad to say that the Mayor's indisposition was only temporary, and they would all agree with him when he said that they earnestly hoped he would be amongst them speedily and in full health and vigour. (Hear, hear.) , WATCH COMMITTEE.

IMPROVEMENTS AT THE NEW POLICE PREMISES At a meeting held on the sth December, a letter wai read from the Home office with respect to the mainten- ance of offenders under the Youthful Offenders Act on remand or pending trial, when it was resolved, that the committee will be prepared to recommend the Council to bear the maintenance of such offenders. At a meeting held on the following day Mr Burns Dick attended and discussed with the committee certain alterations and improvements at the new police premises.—At another meeting on the 19 h December thegollowing letter from Mr C A Hindle, acting on behalf of Messrs Cackett and Burns Dick, was read :—ln reply to your letter of 10th December to the architects. The builders' detailed prices are now to hand. The fol- lowing is a summary of totals :—Move dock, new brass rails, new iron railings, seat and desk in dock, £26 48 3d ; sundries, £2 ; lower floor witness boxes, raise all reporter's sat. raise magistratos' clerk's seat and anoth,r, £lB 153 8d ; sundries, £2 ; form new magistrates' room, doors, divisionson'astering cornice, leaded lights, heating apparatus, £5O 14 43 : sundres, £1 145 ; making a total of £lOO 153 31 It was resolved that the above alterations to the new police premises be carried out at a cost not exceeding the estimates supplied by Mr Hindle, subject to the Borough Surveyor being satisfied as to the details of the work. _ _

The DEPUTY-MAYOR moved, and Alderman SUTTON seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor GREENING asked for information with reference to the alterations to the new police buildings. —How was it that there had been so much bungling ? They were to spend over £lOO in alterations. He was a member of the Watch Committee but he could not get the information. Ile was not a member of the com- mittee when the building was proposed to be erected,but the alterations seemed to be extraordinary. Someone was to blame that all these alterations were required. Alderman Horcnissox : If Councillor Greening had attended the meetings of the committee he need not have asked the question here. The DErcerv-MAron : Toe answer is that the sugges- tions came from toe magistrates who have used the premises from time to time, and it is in deference to the views expressed by them that the Watch Com- mittee have agreed to the proposed expenditure. The resolution was carried. FINANCE AND ESTATE COMMITTEE. THE GAS ANNUITIES.—RE-ORGANISATION OF STAFF.

At a meeting of the Committee, held on the 2nd Deceeber, it was resolved that the Borough Treasurer bseempowered to negotiate withholders of Gas annuities for the conversion thereof into bonds at 30 years pur- chase and bearing 4 per cent. interest for five years cer- tain ; tnereafter at ordinary current rate of interest on Corporation bonds or on such other terms not exceeding the above in amount as he may be able to arrange.—At another meeting. on the 16th, December, Mr iirdliam Boyle. the chief clerk in the Berough Treasurer's department, having been appointed borough accountant of Crewe, and he having requested the Committee to allow him to arrange with Mr Fairhurst as to ths date of giving up his duties under the Corporation. it was rrsolved, that Mr Boyle'a request be acceded to and that in accepting his resignation the Committee con- gratulate him on his appointment, and that the follow- ing report of the Borough Treasurer on the re-erganisa- tion of his staff owing to the appointment of Mr Boyle as borough accountant of Crewe be approved In consequence of the appointment of my Chief Clerk, Mr Boyle, as borough accountant of Crewe, it will be necessary to make arrangements to fill the vacancy. As the office work is continually increasing I feel it necessary to rearrange the department in such a way as to keep it efficient. I consider that this can best be ensured by promoting Mr Houghton, who is neat in position, to be chief clerk, and to give the clerks nest in turn to him more responsible work than they are at present doing, transferring a junior clerk from the rate section, and appointing an PACe boy, if after a little experience this latter should be found neces,ary. Thelvac incy in the rate section to be filledlby:thie appoint meat of a:youth; further by transferring to the asaistant collectors some portion of the work at present done by my particular staff. I think thee that the work would be well distributed and the duties performed satisfac- torily. I consider thislpromotion to more responsible duties a suitable time to give some slight increase in salary, and I suggest that Mr Houghton become chief clerk at a salary of £llO, rising by annual increments to a mooch-num of £lso,and that the other clerks affected have slight inc-eases. These changes will, I feel sure maintain the efileiency of the department, will give satisfaction to the staff, and can be carried out at a financial Ravine of over £3O per annum. Alderman SHLY7 GREEN moved the confirmation of the minutes, and alluded to the resolution that the Treasurer be empowered to negotiate with holders of gas annuities for the conversion thereof into bonds on the terms mentioned in the minutes. There was no power given to them to compel the holders to sell, and the Corporation, realising the predicament, bad deter- mined to make an effort to induce the holders to let them have the bonds by offering them the highest erica at which they were saleable. The Corporation offered, them as an inducement 4 per cent, for a period and they could leave the capital with them for as long a period as they liked on terms to be arranged. They hoped the holders would help them out of the present predicament. Alluding to Mr Boyle, be said they were losing a very valuable servant, but they were pleased to know that another Corporation had realised that there were in him services which might be invaluable to them. He was improv- ing his position, and the committee were conscious that they would have some little difficulty in suitably filling his position. There were other useful and active mem- bers on the staff, and the committee were of opinion that it was the proper policy to give them a chance and they adopted the resolution believing that they would be able to conduct efficiently their work as hitherto. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH seconded. Councillor BENNETT asked if there would be any actual saving with regard to the gas annuities. Alderman SHAW GREEN, in reply, said that, though the re would be some difficulty in replying specifically there would be a saving eventually. They were com- pelled as a committee t 3 offer some inducement to the holders, and in a short time they would be better off for the conversion. The minutes were carried. INCANDESCENT V. ELECTRIC LIGHTING. INSTUETTROEssrrmiNoZdetOhI:PARISONS: Alderman confirmation of the minutes of the Stre.t Improve me and Lighting Com- mittee which contained a resolution that wi and Win wick-road between thenwicx-etreet "witei Horse " Inn and ht. Ann's Church be lighted gh Surveyor .Incandescent gas lamps. The Boron .e to report :—That I he has considered the question of cost (tad suovists that the basis of calculation should be the cost of light- ing 'per mile of street and would compare the electric lighting of Sankey-strevt and Bridge-street with the in- candescent light of Wilderspool Causeway. The number of electric arc lamps in Sankey-street to Market Gate thence down Dridge-street to Friars Green is 13, this in- cluding the two lamps opposite the iron gates to the Town Hall. The distance mentioned is half-a-mile, therefore 26 lamps would be required pet mile. The cost charged for electric lighting in £22 per annum per lamp, which makes:a total of £572 per mile. The arc lamps are turned out at midnight and the glow lamps put on, which of course do not give the Aame power as the arc. The incandeecent lamps on Wildersnool Causeway are spaced about 65'yards apart, which gives 28 lamps per mile. Taking the lamps to be 300 candle power each the cost is £7 54 per annum per lamp, which gives a total cost of £203 per mile per annum burning all night. If the incandescent lights are lowered at midnight as are the arc lights the cost per lamp will be £5 103 or £154 per mile, to which of course must be added the man's time for lowering the lights at say 104 per week, making a total cost per mile per annum of £lBO. The total candle power per mile of arc lights will be 26 x 2,000=52,000 cp. The toz,nl candle power per mile of incandescent lights will be 28 x 300=8,400 c.p. The cost per candle power per annum for the arc lights is 2-64 pence, and for the incandescent lights if lowered at midnight 5.14 pence:per candle power. Yours obediently,Thos LONGDIN. Alderman SUTTON, alluding to Mr Longdin's report, saidehey would see that the cost of incandescent lighting was only one-third that of electric lighting, and the Committee had passed the resolution re Winwick-
strzet in ordes to test further the merits of the two illuminints and see which was preferable. . . .

Councillor BURTON said he 'took it that it was the intention of the Committee zo light the main streets of the Borough with electric light, and also to increase the present lights in the near future. The lights in the main streets at present were too far apart, and it seemed to him to be unfair to those people whose places of business were situated midway between two of the arc lights, because they got very little light. He thought they might have three lights where they now had two. , Finally, Councillor Burton drew attention to the inade- quate lighting of Wilson Patten-street, and said that there were serious complaints of many undesirable characters who walked that street: Alderman SUTTON The sub-committee have the lighting of Wilson Patten-street under cdnsideration. Councillor Trensmsr said he would like to have seen in Mr. bongdin's report, the cost per mile of ordinary lamp., and the cost per candle power. It seemed to him that the incandescent light was much cheaper than the electric, but before they came to any decision they Should know the difference between the incandescent and the ordinary lamp. He hoped Wilson Patten-street would have the same consideration as Winwickestrest. Councillor GREENING said he was much surprised to 890 that the difference between the cost of the two lights was so enormoue. Be thought the committee were quite right in adopting the incandescent because it gave a better light than the arc lamp. He should also like them to take into consideration the intensified gas. The light outside the gas offices was the finest light in War- rington, and it was cheaper thin incandescent. Councillor BENNETT said that if Councillor Greening would read the report he would see that although the cost of the electric light was greater than the incan- descent the power was also much grea:er. Councillor PLIIMPTON s aid in his opinion the incan- descent light could not be improved upon by the electric light. The arc-lights were too far apart and to render the lighting efficient the town would be put to ten times the cost it had been already. Anyone going along Wilderapool-road most admit that the light there could not be improved upon. They wood not carry the electric light much further than it had already gone. Alderman BOLTON rain the electric arc lamps cost £22 per annum each. He thought them too strong for War- riegton streets and suggestea two lights of less power in place of each lamp. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said it seemed to him that the basis of comparison was altogether wrong. If he was right then the candle power of arc tamps' at £572 per mile was equal to the incandescent light at £1,502 per mile for the same candle-po iver. Whichever was the cheaper light seemed to be a matter of figures. Alderman MONKS: That is about it Mr Chairman.

Alderman SUTTON said the Deputy-Mayor's statement was quite correct. Taking the candle power into con- sideratioa the electric light was cheaper, bat they thought the incaldescent was the best light for the streets. The Boroagh Surveyor bad gone into the matter very fully and they found from actual experience that they could have the streets lighted with incandescent light at about one third the cost of electric light. The minutes were confirmed. HEALTH COMET TEE—AR. FLOOD'S APPOINTMENT.

Alderman Sorrov said they had now definitely ap- p)in ted Mr W T Flood as chief insoector at £l2O per annum, the salary to increass £lO yearly until a maiirnum of £2OO was reached. The lats Inspector Norman was in receipt of £2DD at the tim a of his death.
The DEPUTY- VAYOR seconded the &dentine of the miuntcs proposed by Aid...win SattJe, and the metion was carried. ALDERMAN MONKS REIGN S TFIE CHAIRMAN- SHIP OF THE SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE.

Councillor JOHN EVANS pronosed the adoAion of the minutes of the above Commi:t ,e which csntained the following resolution :—"That the Committee desire to record their appreciation of the valuable services ren- dered be Mr Alderman Monks during his chairmanship of the Committee for the last nine years, and their expression of regret on his retirement from that posi- tion." Counc llor Evans sail he had especial pleasure in asking them t confirm this resolution, and he hardly thought he need say more. He was voicing the opinion of every member of the Council when he said they toped Mr Monks would remain with them many years as a member of the Committse. (Rear, _hear). _ _

, COalleillOT GREENING seconded and said be muse add his testimony to the very valuable work done by Alderman Monks. He had sat under Alderman Monks for many years, and he could testify to his doing every: thing thoroughly. The sanitary condition of Warrington to-day was eloquent testimony to the work he had done. The speaker was sorry, with all deference to the new chairman,that Alderman Monks had resigned, though he was sure the Committee would prosper as much in the future under the ohairmanship of Councillor John Evans as it had done in the past. (13,ar, bear). The DEPUTY-MAYOR endorsed all that bad tom said• Lie had been es member of the Sanitary Work; Com- mittee since its formatioo and had had a good deal to do with getting Alderman Monks to be Ceairmsn, and that selection had proved to be a very wise one. The manner in which Alderman Monks had devoted himself to what was then a very difficult problem reflected very great credit upon him and made the town his debtor. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was carried unanimotply. liderrnan MONK 3 in reply texpressed his gratitude to the Council and committee for having placed this matter on record. It was vary gratifying to him to receive this further mark of their confidence. He did not take too much to himself because he had felt that all the success was not due to him. The committee bad most loyally backed him up in the difficult times they had had to face. It was plain sailing now but he could remember when thines were very different and they had as many different opinions on matters as there were members of the committee. He would say, however, that the minority would always give way and then do their best to support the majority. That went to a large extent to the success of the efforts of the com- mittee to put the sanitary affairs of the town en a better footing, He could recommend other committees to follow on similar lines. In conclusion Alderman Monks thanked the members very much for their expressions of confidence. (Applause). PAVING AND SEWERAGE covimirrEE.—A CON-

A rather remarkable occurence on Croston-street, Beswick, Manchester, recently has created something of a sensation in the neighbourhood. Fir about twelve months No. 45, has been teoanted by Mr. Wood, an employ of the Great Northern Railway Co., whose daughter, Marjorie Eva, now five years of age, has, within that period, undergone an experience to which it would be difll t.alt to find a parallel. A Manchester reporter, in order to verify what had come to ,his knowledge, called upon Mrs. Wood a few days ago, and took from her own lips the following facts. " Before my daughter, Marj irie, was five years of age she began to exhibit peculiar twitchings of the muscles of the hands and arms, which in time extended to the face, the eyes, and mouth. She also used to complain of her legs aching, and soowod signs of languor and weariness. When in bed at nights there was a twitching of the limbs, accompanied by great restlessness. For some time I thought it was a bad habit she had got iota, and that she would soon get over it. As the symptom a grew gradually worse, I became alarmed and took her to a. doctor, who teld me she was afflietediwith St. Vitus' Dance. He prescribed for her, and the chili took his medi- cine, Lut as far as I could see it did her no good whatever. She got worse. I was walking out with Marjorie one day when her condition attracted Vie attention of a lady, who was passing. Tne lady asked me if I had not taken the girl to a doctor. I replied that I had done so, and that he had told me she was suffering from St. Vitus' Dance ; that he had prescribed for her, but hie medicines had made her no better. The lady then said : ' I know a little girl who had St. Vitus' Dance,. who was cured by taking Dr.:Williams' Pink Phis for Pale People.' I said I had heard of them, but had not taken any. What the lady had said, however, induced me to try a box. Before the girl had taken half the pills I noticed a great improvement. In fact, she began tosget better after the first two or three pills." " How many boxes did she take ? "

" Only one box. One box quite cured her." " It seems a remarkable cure. because young girls affected with St. Vitus Dance seldom get better before a certain stage of life is reached." "And so I think," said Mrs Wood with fervency, " and I:was so delighted that I wro'e to Dr. Williams medicine cornpany,and told them that 'words could not express the pleasure I felt in doing so."
AT OTHER TIMES of life—when headaches, tired back, delayed development, trouble the parents of THE GROWING GIRL, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills will help her to

it may be just your girl's case. BLACKBURN GIRL HELPED IN A TRYING TIME.

Miss Elsie Winifred Carter is ready to admit that a little inquisitiveness on her part proved m-re valuabls than she ever anticipated. This young lady lives with her mother and sister at SS, Bolton-road, Blackburn. In conversation with a reporter from the " Blackburn Standard and Express " Miss Carter, said :" I have twice broken down in health in August, which is the end of the season. I used to come home at night from my work feeling very sickly and exhausted, and everyone commented on my pale appearance. This went on unchecked until I became completely run down. Though I took medicine it seemed to have no effect what- ever upon me." At this point Mrs. Carter, interposed. " Many a morning I :have heard her say, wearily, "Oh. I wish I was not going to work, I am so tired already." In her spare moments she would fall asleep and yet wake up even more exhausted: But I will tell you how the trouble was conquered. In my shop (• chemists) I sell Dr Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, you know, and I had decided to take some of them myself. I opened a box and left it in a drawer in the shop. I subsequently ncticed that my daughter seemed to be getting over her illness quite remarkably, and one day:when I went to use the box of pills I found it empty. I made hoquiries,and Elsie told me she bad taken them all, unknown to:us, and she felt certain her improvement in health was due to Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

" Naturally," continued Mrs. Carter," we were delighted with the result of my dear girl's inquisitiveness which led her to try the pills. She continued to take them, with the result that she has quite recovered be wonted health and strength, and the colour has returned to her cheeks." " How many boxes did you take altogether 9" asked the interviewer. "Three boxes in all,"teplied Miss Carter,"and I feel like a different being,and I can now do my work as a dress maker without the tired feeling, while the heavy depression has quite vanished and I feel well and cheerful. •

Mr, Alexander Wood, of 59, Bankhall-street, liirkdale, Everpool• is a gentleman, woo in Ms desire to be well fortunately followed a right course. The matter was fully investigated by a leading Liverpool paper, the re-' porter of which writes of it as follows:—.6 Tall and powerfully built is Mr Wood. ' I have spent twentp-eight years at sea as cook and steward,' he told me, ' and the sea left Me an unwelcome and painful legacy. I did a lot of cooking by steam, and the draughts in the galleys with the damp steam seemed to settle a cold on my shoulders. Rheumatism was the result, and I've also had sciatica. It is eight years new since I stopped on shore, and regularly every winter I've been laid up for three or tour days or a week. I couldn't lift my right arm above my shoulder. Besides that, I suffered from a terrible languid and drowsy feeling, chiefly in my legs, I was as tired when I got up in the morning as when I went to bed at night. I spent many a pound on doctors, but nothing seemed to do me permanent good. Every winter I was laid up until this year. Finally I picked up a little book about Dr. Pink Pills for Pale People, and I thought to myself—" give .this a trial." Six weeks ago I began taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills with constantly increasing improvement. See that arm '—and Mr Wood moved his right arm about—' I can do anything with it. I was never any good without wearing a belt round my waist. I wear no belt now. I feel ten years younger, and as well as anybody peed feel. In this wet weather I should have been laid up directly, but cow, thsnks to Dr. Williams' Pink fills for Pale People, I'm going about my work as well and as regularly as possible.' "

Mrs Agnes Sherrock, of 85, Milton-street, Burnley, whose story has recently been the subject of much gossip in the Fu'ledge district where she lives, is forty-one years of age and employed as a weaver. She was waited upon the other day by a representative of the Burn/ey Gazdte, to whom she freely gave the particulars of a remarkable escape. •• Some time ago," she said, "I was !aft in a prostrate condition. I lost a great dcal of blood and for years was unable to get any relief. I was under three or four doctors in all," she said, " but my improvement was not marked. I was always getting off my work through weakness. At one time I was ao home over three years. being too weak to attempt to go to the mill. I got So bad with palpitation of the heart that if I tried to do a hit of housework, I had to stop every few minutes. If I walked a short distance from the door I was done up and had to get back as best I could. My husband had to carry rue upstairs as I could not get up myself. During all this time I lost all kkigg for foed and could scarcely eat anything, and if I did I felt painful indigestion after it. I lost all desire to go out or do anything even in the house. I was under four doctors altogether, and about twelve months since I was recommended as a last resource to go into the hospital. I was here about ten weeks, and then I found that they intended to operate upon rue, but they considered I was too weak to undergo an oper- ation and so they brought rue home again. When I had been home from the hospital about six weeks, my' husband thought we should try some of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.
