WUPCIIIOI' BENNETT asked for an exp'antt,oa of the resolution—" That the B irourh S irvevor be authorised to purchase two truck loads of kerbs from Messrs Bennie and Thompson and John Pendlebury and Co., at the prices named in their respective tenders, and that the remainder of the order be given to tie firm supply- ing the best quality of sample kern. Councillor PLIMPTON sail the two firms te id; red fir the contract at the same once, and as they did not state definitely what make the kerbs were the committee decided to have a truck load of eaco and leave the Borough Surveyor to exercise his j aigment as to which was the best. Carried. MUSEUM COMMIT rEE —CHANGES IN THE STAFF. The I)En:cry-Mayon proposed the adoption of the minutes of the MUSeLltil, ST,,, Cllntriittee,Which included the following items : Resolved that Artour Deane be appointed assistant curator at £6O a year salary, rising £lO yearly to £l2O ; one month's notice to terminate the engagement 1 Resolved that the following tenders for work at the new Technical School be accepted :—Messrs Smith, South- port, for Electric Light Installation, £3lO Ils . Messrs Saunders and Taylor for heating apparatus, £489. ; Messrs Shrigley and Hurst for stained glass. 104 per vinare foot. The following report of II M. Inspector on the Commercial and Continuation Classes last vssion was read :—" The staff is a well chosen one, and highly efficient, In all subjects regular and continuoua advance was made during the session, and all Subjects, with the exception of Latin and Spanish, found a satisfactory number of diligent and earnest pupils." •.' In moving the adoption:of the mintPes, the Deputy. Mayor said they bad another instance of the training of a Warrington youth resulting in his getting another appointment. Mr A Dean was appointed assistant curator owing to the resignation of Mr E Lowe, who was practically trained in the Warrin2ton Museum and had obtained an important post in Plymouth. He was a splendid workman and one whom ho 13 lived had an important future loz.fors him. Councillor GREENING seconded and the minutes were confirmed. MARKETS COMMITTEE—ITINERANT VENDORS TO

BE CHECKED. Oa the minutes of the above committee was a refer- ence to a petitiol siened by a 'aryl number of stall- holders askinß for restrictions to be put upon the use of the markets by itinerant vendors. Resolved that the rents of the stalls on the south side of the market be Increased to 64 per aves,k as ane from Ist January. 1902. .Ilderrnan HUTCHINSON moved the adoptim of the minutes.

COURCiIIOr ROGERS seconded. Alderman Sn-rror said he thought the grievance one that 0u413t to be retnedied and ho would suggest that vendorg of produce ghoul i have the first consideration, , a wares should come last. They effected that vend Ors °d" e Off ected the the shopkeepers and paid no rates in the town. Councillor W ROBERTS : The memorial refers more hn o particularly to auctioneers who come. (Laucelter.) Alderman SurroN : All the better for me then. (More laughter.) Councillor W ROBERTS said these people were careful to select the time of the year when there was a bit of ready money knocking about, and they came to the very great disadvantage of people who were in the market all the year round. Councillor GREENING : The buyers or the sellers ? The minutes were confirmed. THE NEW OAS OFFICES.
The Gag Committee recgmmendel that the plan of the alteration to the offices necessitated by part of the premises being required for tramway purposes now sub-

rmitted be approved and that tenders be obtained for the work.—air S Percy Silcock reported that be valued the land and buildings at the old gas works required by the Tramways Depsrtment at £2,340. letilla.R FAIRCLOUGH said the committee wished the plan to be referred beck for further consideration. Be proposed the confirmation of the minutes. Aldermen BOLTON seconded and celled attention to the action of the committee in asking Mr Percy Silcock to value the premiaes at the old gas works required by the Tramways Committee. Be thought the Borough Surveyor ought to have valued it and fixed a fair price between the two committees. Not only had the Gas Committee called in Mr Silcoak, but he saw from the minutes of the Tramways Committee that that Com- mittee had asked Mr William Owen to value the land and buildings for them. The result was that two out- side valuers had been celled in when the Borough Sur- veyor might have done the work. Counciller BENNETT Celled attention to the minute of the committee wnich reed " Toe engineer was em- powered to: purchase 150 tons of Arley slack on the terms seti out in his report of this day." He wanted to know why the terms were not stated. Alderman MONKS said although the plans of new offices had been withdrawn, he thought it was worth while mentioning that it had been discussed whether it would not be wise and more economical to remove some of the staff at present located at M-rsey-street to Bank House or some other office more convenient. He thought there was something in toe idea, It had never been definitely proposed because there was an idea that there was opposition to such a senetree. Belore the plans were approved he thought they ought to consider whether economy could be effected by removing the office' to Bank House. Alderman Faraceocron said the Gas Committee had discussed the matter time after time. The plans which the committee intended to submit for the approval of the Council at the next meeting would last the coin- mittee for the next twelve years. Something would have to be done in the meantime to bring all the offices of the Corporation near the Town Hall. With regard to Councillor Bennett's, question respecting the purchase of 150 tons of slack, he wished to state that occasions occurred when they had to purchase outside their usual contracts. Owing to the frost and fog, the demand for gas was enormous and as they were unable to get suffi- cient fuel from the contractors to enable them to meet the demand, the gas engineer wee instructed to pur- chase the 150 tone of Arley slack. It was obtained at less cost than the contract price. The minutes were then confirmed. THE STATE OF THE RIVER. The Rivers Committee reported that the Borough Sur- veyor notified that considerable erosion was taking place in the river embankment on Chester-road. The DEPUTY MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes. Alderman Hurcareson seconded. Council ir GREENING expressed his disappointment with the minutes of the Rivers Cernmittee month by month. They never had any information concerning the work in the river. He hoped the Rivers Committee were mov ng in the matter and were determine to insist upon the river being kept in a proper condition. Be was certai% that if the committee came forward ' with some scheme To deal with the work they would have the support of the whole Council. (Hear, hear). The DEPUTY Mayne said the committee had learned , one or two lessons during the last few years and one of the lessons was not to tell the other side everything they were doing. They would come before the Ceuacil very soon with the proposal to take active measures to insist upon the rights of Warrington being preserved in cennecton with the river. The minutes were approved. ELECTRICITY. The Electricity Committee proposed that the tender of Mr Joseph Dolan for concrete engine bed and switch- board platform extension at £169 be accepted. ' Alderman MONKS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, stated that satisfactory arrangements had been made with the Whitecross Company Limited to supply current for motive power. There were indica- tioee that other manufacturers in the town would use electric current and there was every probability of their scheme for hiring motors cat thing on and being a financial succeee. Arrangements had been made for two extra shifts in view of the introduction of the tram- ways and also to enable the committee to supply cur- rent for all requirements at any hour. Alderman FAIRCLOUGEI seconded the adoption of the minutes which were confirmed. THE TRAMWAYS UNDERTAKING. The Tramways Committee recommended that the tender of Mr J A Ewart for the con- struction of the permanent way for carsheds at £1,155 be accepted. A letter was read from the' British Electric Traction Company, Limited, respecting the leasing of the tramways. The Town Clerk was in itrotted to inform the Company that if they would submit their proposals with respect to leasing in writ- ing, the same should be considered at an early date. It was resolved that Mr W H Grimsdale be appointed (pro tem) the manager of the Tramways Department at a salary of £lOO per annum. The DEPUTY-MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman MONKS seconded. Alderman BOLTON alluded to a resolution of the corn- ' mittee requesting Mr William Owen to make a valua- tion of the land and buildings at the old gas works required for car sheds. Be moved an amendment that the minute be struck out. He-did not See why they should have two valuers and perhaps three or four arbitrators to decide the value of a bit of land to be transferred from onetcommittee to another. He was expecting the Deputy-Mayor to give some explanation. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH isFconded the amendment. , Couneillor JAXIES EVANS asked the Deputy-Mayor to ' give an explanation. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said the facts were these. The Gas Committee had some land which the Tramways Committee desired to purchase. The Gas Committee called in Mr Percy Silcoak to make a valuation on their behalf. The Tramways Committee reeeived the vial a- tion, and theee was a division 'of opinion as to whether it was a reasonable one or a high one. In order to put themselves absolutely right as business men they thought it better to instruct an architect to make a valuation on their account, which they had a perfect right to do. Alderman Bolton had said it made no differ- ence when the transfer was between one committee and another. It made a material difference, because tbe price paid has to be added tn the capital account, and if:they gave £lOOO rr o e than it was worth, that amount was sadoled on the Tramways Committee, and tveuld have to be paid out of the tramways undertaking. rho Committee had called in Mr Owen, and he believed they had got his valuation. Alderman Feraceomen said in that case ha would withdraw from seconding the amendment. Alderman BOLTON did net think money ought to be thrown away in the employment of architect,. Councillor TINNION thought both the Gee Committee and the Tramways Committee bad made a mistake. The proper course was to call in the Borough Surveyor' and ask him to give a valuation. Alderman SUTTON said it was the first time to his knowledge that two committees of the Corporation had called in outside valuers to value a piece of property as between one committee and another. So far as the rate- payers were concerned the traesfer was taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another. Be hoped that the Botoueh Surveyor would be called in in any future case. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said the initial blunder was not with the Tramways Committee. That committee acted first and called in Mr Percy Sileock. The Tramways Committee would have put the Borough Surveyor in a very awkward position if they bad asked him to make a valuation against an outside valuer. Therefore the committee called in Mr Owen. Personally he (the Deputy-Mayer) would have leeen pleased to have left the whole:question with the Borough Surveyor. Tee Tramways Committee was not going to buy land from the Corporation or anybody else at a higher figure than it was worth. Conneillor BENNETT : Yon have created two fees as between one committee and another. The DEPUTY-StAYOR said whatever stun was paid for the land and buildings, it would have to come out of the aevenuellof the tramways. How could they be expected to pay if the committee had to pay through the rose ? Councillor BENNETT : You relieve the Gas Committee of that amount Alderman RoBERTS : We don't want to relieve the Gas Committee. Councillor PIERPOINT asked whether tbere were only two valuers in Warrington and what amount of com- mission was being paid by the Gas Committee on the eine hand and the Tramways Committee on the other. If they pet it down that they were going to pay a modest one per cent. it seemed to him that on Mr Percy Sileock's valuation they weuldi havejto pay £23. Re thought they ought to have advertised for a tender for the valuing of these perticular works, (Laughter, and a Voice : Sealed tender ?) Sealed tender or unasaled he did not earn which but he hoped the members of the Connell would remember the fact that they had more than one architect in the town and more .than two valuere.

TUE APPOINTMENT OF TRAMWAYS M ANAGER. Councillor JLTAES Eves called the attention of the Council to the resolution of the committee that Mr W H Grimsda!e be appointed (pro. tern ) the manager of the Tramways Department at a salary of £lOO per annum. fle said that whilst he had nothing at all to say against Mr Grimsdale who was present in the room,and his ap- preciation of that gentleman's services as electric engineer was (pita as great as actoone else's, he took exception to the procedure, not as against Mr Grime- dale, but on principle. ll' did not think in the fret place that it was economic to the ratepayers that any official of the Corporation should hold two positiens under different committees and conduct two different 1 departments. It might be e3nnomic in the initial stage but he thought it ended in deputies being appointed who ran up salaries of the management ti a considerable sum Be was somewhat surprised when he saw the suggestion of the appointment, for the Council must remember that a very few months ago Alderman Monks made a vary smart speech with regard to Mr Grimsdile and the extra work he would have

I put upon him in selling motors and pushing trade in that direction in the interests of the ratepayers, to make the electric undertaking a paying concern. A deputy was appoitate I at a salary of £l3O and to this he (the speaker) gave his consent. The Electric Cern- ranee was now proposing to increase the res pos. I )1 i lee of the electrical engineer by two shifts in every 24 hours and was going to employ a considerable additional number of men, and he took it that this would increase Mr Grimsdale's responsibilities at the works. Another point waich he wished to raise was that he believed it would be in the interests of the ratepayers if the position were advertised. He believed it ought to be advertised, and if they offered this situation they would have as many applications from efficient men as they were going to offer pounds per annum as salary. He maintained that Mr Grimsdale's appointment was keeping some other good man out of what he (the speaker) looked upon as a good situation. The sum total of it meant in pram'ple that someone got the beef and someone got the bone. (Laughter). In every place be found as a rule that somebody with some practical know ledge and good common sense was engaged as a deputy. He did not say it would be so in this case. He hoped it would not be taken that he was insinuating, but it was commonly said that they ceuld buy good brains at thirty shillings a week. Is Alderman ROBERTS : Of a sort. Councilior EVANS You can buy gend ones. There are good brains under many a rough skull. (Laughter). Continuing the speaker said that in the interests of the ratepayers the position should be advertised and the Tramways Committee shou'd make its selection of an independent man with practical knowledge of the con- ducting of tramways. He moved an amendment that the minutes of the committee be passed with the excep- tion of that resolution. Councillor WILKINSON sezonded. UP always felt strongly, he said. against any offizial holding a dual position in the Corporation. It could not tend to the development of any department. Councillor Wrerreet ROBERTS said he noticed that in the minute it said tee appointment was pro teat. ; COUtlCillOr EVANS: We know what pro ten means. We have had a lot of pro tem. Councillor Was ROBERTS said that protably sem& infer- mation mish ;be given on the point which would influence the Council in coming to a decision. From his personal know edee of what was before them, he should not like for one moment to vote against a temporary appoint- ment. However much he might be opposed to a dual appointment as a permanency it might be simply in- tended that the appointment should remain in force until the tramways were in proper working order—(a voice : "No ")• They hod a perfect right to their opinion so had he. So far as any dual appointments already:existed in the Corporation he did not think anyone had aoy reason to complain. They had a dual appointment in the case of Mr Dees. COURCiIIOr JAMES EVANS It iS & matter of principle. A VOICE: Keep to the point. • Councillor W Bonsai's : It is to the point I think. Mr Dees is water engineer and is also responsible for the management of Le.ngford. Councillor JAMES Evess : I rise to a point of order. I am net making invidious comparisons at all. Couneill W ROBERTS : You spoke against dual appointments. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Tne observation is perfectly in order. I did not call you (Councillor Evans) to order when you referred to dual appointments. The principle is open to discussion. Continuing, Councillor W ROBERTS said they had an illustration in that particular case of the fact that al dual appointment was not always a thing to be con- dem led. Although he had not been in the Council long he had taken a deep interest in Council affairs and ever since the dual appointment ot Mr Deas was made he had never read or heard of soy objection or complaint about the way in which he had discharged his duty. So far as Mr Grims late was concerned he was perfectly sure that what they all knew of him was certainly in his favour and if the appointment was only a tempor- ary one he (the speaker) should certainly give it his cordial support. Councillor FORSHAW agreed with the observations of Councillor Evans. It was very undesirable that the Corporation should appoint an official to a double office. Is was wrong in principle and under these circum- stances he should support the amendment. Councillor PIERPOINT (to the Daputy-Mayor : Before the Council ernes to the vote will yoa kindly give some information ? The DEPUTY-MAYOR : I should have been very glad if the gentlemen with that common sense which usually characterises members of the Council had abstained from giving a drfieite view till af:er the explanation Continuing, he said they had a very serious proposal before them, or rather something that would lead to a very serious proposal from the British Electric Traction Company, Ltd. As they were aware, some months ago the Company approached them with a view to leasing the tramways from the Corporation. At that time the Corporation decided that they would make the tram- ways themselves, !raving open for consideration the question of whether they would lease them to the Com- pany or nor. He could say that speaking for himself, whenever ho finally gave his vote on the question of leasing the tramways or not, he should feel that he was taking perhaps the most serious responsibility connected with the committee that had yet come up for ' consideration. Having in view the possibility of the early discussion of these proposals and also knowing Ithe fact that probably within two months from now the tramways, so far as Latchford: and Sankey Bridges were concerned, would be running, it was necessary to make some provision of a purely temporary character to carry on the management. Mr. Grimsdale's appoint- ment was absolutely a temporary one and he believed he was right in saying it was subject to a month's notice to terminate it. There were many reasons why it was desirable that they should not commit themselves to any serious extent in regard to the management till they had decided whether they were going to manage the tramways themselves or lease them to the company. That was the whole explanation. The amendment was then put to the meeting and defeated by a large majority. The Council then proceeded to discuss the Municipal Trading qaestion. A.: report of the discussion is given in another column.

div.p: ITIE EXAMINEE, FRID A le. JANUARY 10 1902.
TOWN versus COUNTRY.

The tendency of mankind is more and more towards aggregation in great cities. Persistent depression .of the agricultural industry, and the quickening of social instinct due to improved education, are the chief causes of this phenomenon. Modern folks will read with plea- sure (in fiction) of the house on the marsh, and some- times sing of a cottage near a wood ; but they decline to live in either. They prefer the crowded city, with its mills and factories and bustling market place. In this they are both losers and gainers. An English oak is pleasanter to look upon than a tall smoke stack : but it provides nothing towards boiling the pot but such branches SP the winter gales detach from it ; whereas the fumes from the factory chimney, though they clog the bronchial tubes, provide gold for the household purse. No smoke, no work ;no work, no pay ;no pay, no food—such is the declension so well understood by the telling Yes, the smoke of a large city is a bad thing for bronchial affection, and unfortunately Stockport is well supplied with it. Mrs Elizabeth Elhirt,a widow,63 years of age, of ffibbert-street, Newtown, New Mills, near Stock pert,says : "For 20 years I was subject to bronchitis and indigestion. My breathing was bad, and as soon as the cold and wet c,f winter set in I was laid up. In Dec., 1597, influenza was added to my troubles and my con- dition became critical. Whatever I ate made me sick or caused a sinking pain in the chest. A hard, dry cough used to literally shake me. Sometimes these coughing fits would last until I was black in the face,and covered with perspiration. Often I feared I should burst a blood vessel. My sleep was spoilt by it,and I became so weak that only to walk across the room exhausted me." The doctors evidently found this a difficult case. Mrs Shirt continues:: " For a long time the doctor attended me; but as his medicine did me no good, I gave over taking it, and decided to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. From Itbe very first bottle my condition improved, and the improvement continued until I was completely cured. For four years I have been untroubled by bronchitis or indigestion, and lam in better health now than at any time during the previous 20 years." Considering the number of victims which broncbitis annually claims, more specially amon; those who have passed the middle stage of life, this is grand evidence, and fully justifies Mrs Shirt's concluding remarks : "If ever I feel a little out of sorts, a few doses of Mother Qeigel's Curative Syrup invariably puts me right again. I cannot speak well enough of it, and hope my testi- mony may induce others to try it."

SOME wise persons have The Progress of the War, compiled a summary of Lord KITCHENER'S opera- tions for the year just ended, and in the concrete form the figures go to show pretty conclusively that our position is very different from what it was twelve months ago. The CommaNnen-rx- CHIEF accounts for more than 18,000 of the enemy in that period, some 11,000 of this number having - been taken prisoners, while more than 3,009 have surrendered, some 2,000 have been killed, and 1,500 wounded. The statistics confirm emphatic- ally the observation of Sir EDWARD GREY at New- castle this week is to the mistaken policy of pro- clamations. The only proclamation worth retain- ing, said Sir EnwAan,was annexing the territories of the two colonies. As a matter of fact, the attempt to make the enemy surrender under threat of various penalties had an entirely opposite effect to that which was intended. Until August last the Boersiwere surrendering on an average at the rate of about 300 a month. From that time they declined, the total for September being only 393, for October 197, for Novem- ber 93, and for December 121. We are able now to put a proper appreciation on the extravagant cablegrams of some of the war correspondents, which deluded the public with the ide3 that the enemy, cowed and utterly depressed by these fulminations on paper, was yielding its best strength every day. The suggestion of banishment of the Boer Generals, so far from causing them to relax their efforts,made them des- perate, and quickened in their following the pond of sympathy which the irritations of the campaign were causing to be relaxed. The fact remains, however, that by dint of sheer hard, persistent fighting Lord KITCHENER has in the twelve months reduced the Boer strength by 18,000 men. There have been errors in estimating the remnant of the enemy's forces because these deductions are made from hypothetical figures, and figures which are liable to ,expansion by additions tfrom Cape Colony and other sources. But the COMMANDER- IN-CHIEF practically pledges his reputation as to the accuracy of his returns of killed,wounded, sur- renders, and captures, because of the care taken in eliminating doubtful reports. They represent only the personal observation of responsible British officers,and have no " native " colouring. In another respect the report of Lord KITCHENER in this accumulation of details are satisfactory, and that is in regard to the capture of gone. Twenty- seven have been taken during the year, most in the first half; and the situation has been so changed that military critics have been seriously arguing whether we ourselves should not now fight better without guns, because, the Boers haying lost theirs, we are in no danger from artil- lery, and our own heavy weapons delay pursuit. It is noted that, although more than 18,000 Boers have been.accounted for, the rifles secured by us from the enemy number fewer than 8,000. In the early stages of the campaign the Boers used to go through a little theatrical formula on surrender- ing. They apparently had always available dummy weapons for, the purpose—obsolete fusty things_ and the really useful modern rifles they carefully concealed before the final act. In the exigenci of the warfare in its later periods they have n been able to oblige our war correspondents wii these picturesque effects ; the surrenders law been comparatively few, and in the engagemen when a Boer has been killed his fellow-fighter h been careful to look to the economy of the paign whenever possible, and take away his for the benefit of the others. The mystery, course, is how the Boers have been al to keep up their supply of ammunith All the talk about stores being secret
ate ias
cam
rifle
.I , , I . v
=RV

landed from vessels may be dismissed as idle, No doubt the enemy has drawn upon resources which have been concealed discreetly, and no doubt they have been sparing in their expendi, tare. But the whisper is going round that the Boers are indebted to no small extent for their supplies to those engagements which we call
_ "regrettable incidents," and which are especially regrettable on that account. The shortness of the
messages describing these events is only rivalled by their ambiguity, two qualities not often

_ associated. There can be but one reason why the Boers, with their reduced numbers, and maintain- ing the same desire to prolong the campaign, should make such desperate attacks as they do. It does not help them that they inflict more in- jury than we do, or that when the facts come out it is found in many instances that our casualty list is much heavier than theirs. They cannot with their comparatively small numbers afford such victories. Their only justification for these sallies is that they are getting short of ammuni- tion, and they must do these things in order to
get material on sorne occasions. It is said now

that the commandos in the field are reduced to about 2,000 men; but 5,000 seems to be nearer the mark. Allowing for the scope of movement which the country ofTars them, it is incredible that these bands should not be cleared away, if not captured, before long. General FRENCH sends home a most satisfactory account from Cape Colony, and a few more weeks' work should pro- duce almost as good a state of things in the dis- tricts of the Transvaal still disturbed. Then the serious problenas of administration will begin to unfold themselves.

IT is to be regretted that The Decline in the Evening Schools. Dr MACNAMARA. adopts such a strident note in his declamation against the Government's educa- tional policy. His case is strong enough if stated quite plainly, without bitterness. Politiciaus, however, should not assume that the method of controversy is due to party feeling ; it is due rather to his experience as a teacher of the irrita- tion caused among School Board authorities by the check of the Board above. Faw critics of the Government will go so far as Dr MACNAMARA in believing that the Government intended by its legislation of last year to prejudice night schools ; but evil is wrought by want of thought, and the
anxiety of the Duke of DEIiONSHIRE and Sir JOHN GORST to protect voluntary schools seems to dull them to every other consideration,Dr MACNA...
as editor of the Schoo/inaster,collected some few days since information from 132 School Boards as to the work of the present winter ses- sion. Most of the large authorities are included
in the return. Up to October, 1900—that is, for

the 1900-1 session--the enrolments numbered 224,141. Up to last October, for the 1901-2 session, they reached only 190,363. This shows a diminution of 34,003 pupils, or a rough estimate of a drop for the entire count of 100,000. The Act of Parliament of last year was, as its:limit of operation—twelve months
Ltry f ,

—indicates, intended only as a temporary relief from the embarrassments of the Cockerton judg- ment, and the Education Board would have been wise had it been content to leave the School Boards their old discretionary power, at lesst until they could have shewn by a measure this ses- sion that they were prepared to deal generously with the whole question of secondary education. As it is, however, some deplorable lapses have occurred. The Town or aunty Council having been]made the controller of the work of the School Board there has, in several instances, been fric-
tion ; and in some others the Boards knowing the opinions of the Councils, hive abandoned classes.

It is interesting to notice, by the way, that the Leeds City Council de.ilinecl to permit the School Board to make any extension of last year's scheme, but approved of the opening of no fewer than twenty-four new evening schools by the Leeds Church Day Schools Association. Dr. AIACNAMAILA C pmments on this in reference to Sir JOHN GORST'S claim for his measure that it would prevent over- lapping. Tile note summing up the situation at Plymouth is that " all physical exercises are dropped because of the withdrawal of grants for the subject," and in other parts of the
_ country physical exercises seem to have been
discouraged. The fact come rather avvkwardly at a womit when the difficulties of recruiting

are just beginning to make themselves felt, not from lack of applicants, but from their physical defects. Two only out of five who are willing to enlist are fit to make soldiers; and althoUgh the. figures do not stand out so badly for the navy there is an increasing anxiety as to its manning: In these circumstances, it is hardly surprising that one of the most prominent articles in the reviews this month should be devoted to a proposal for compulsory exercises as a part of education in order to: stay the decline of virility. It is.' an interesting commentary on Sir Jon GORST'S cynicisms, which, directed mainly against dancing have had a much wider restrictive influence. But that, of course, is but one of the effects of the chilling influence of the Department as it was exercised last year. In Lmdon the num oer of students of all classes is this session 8,000 less than last year, though hitherto it has been a steadily ascending number. All through the country com- plaints are bein— g made of the invasion of the foreign clerk: From the metropolis he is passing steadily to the larger provincial towns, and, in time, he will find his way into the smaller ones: Ils wants slight guerdon, as he comes to make himself thereughly familiar with our language,and so prepare himself for the tussle for our Colonial trade when he is serving again in his own land. Englishmen cannot be induced to serve abroad on such terms, but they may be quickened by evening schools. The lesson we i Should learn, moreover, is that it s not wiss to be too rigid in requiring that all taught in these schools shall come severely within old-fashioned definitions of education. The aim of education should, after all, be to draw out. and especially to enable us to meet our quickwitted rivals the Americans. It is better there should be a little waste and a little overlapping if thereby moin people could be induced to take an interest knowledge. This, however, is what the Duke of DEVONSHIRE and Sir JOIIN Gortsr cannot be got to understand. The interesting question is whether the discouraging condition of the evening schools this session will have any effect upon them in framing their Bill for the coming session. That seems too much to hope for.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. ---- [BY A CORRESPONDENT. 3
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. ---- [BY A CORRESPONDENT. 3

The Board meeting on Tbursday night from a public point of view was really no meeting at all. The Board was. but barely opened when Mr Cunningham's motion—which was meant to deter- mine the cost on the rates of the transfer of the Wesleyan Schools on the town—came on the tapis. To the astonishment of the pressmen present the meeting resolved on the proposition of a leading voluntaryiot and progressive to thrash the matter out in committee. Accordingly the reporters were requested to re'ire, and, being sensible men,retired from the building altogether so that the members of the Board might work their own sweet will in their own sweet way. Rumour has it that the Imembers were trying to convince each other on the veracity of figures until 11.30 p.m. so that it was las well, perhaps, that the pressmen did retire.

To an impartial mind this committ3e business seems decidedly unfair. 'there are of course many matters which it is the absolute duty of members to discuss in committee as it would be mo.t nn- business like to prematurely disclose information to the public. Bdt hare is a subject upon which the election was fought. The subject involves two conflicting opinions about a set of tigues—not given to the public—about which there should not be a moment's difficulty to one skilled in calcula- tions. And yet the Board actually discuss the thing in camera and adjourn still in committee until Monday evening, when after further discussion re- porters were admitted and the matter given V) the public.

The reporters had been informed that the Pro- gressives only agreed to the meeting going in com- mittee oa the understanding that it was for a few minutes only. But it ehoula be remembered that it is decidedly unpleasant for reporters to retire for 'an uncertain ten minutos to wait until it pleases the Board to readmit them. Especially, too, when the ten minutes may lengthen out into three hours. However, the sets ot figures are now before the public and it is to be hoped that the con- troversy very soon will be at an end.

--- What a " comedy of errors" has bE'en the action of the Church party in regar 1 to the transfer of the Wesleyan Schools to the School Board of Run- corn. From flower to flower sipping honey fits the busy bee. from error to error have travelled the church candidates,gathering remorse and disgust by the way. Canon Wood's first statement was that the transfer of the iVesleyan schools had cost the rates 41 in the .£ and a capital outlay of £4,500. Left no loophole by the challenge of Mr Norman, he dropped the capital outlay and reduced the charge on the rates to a penny. Now Mr Cunning- ham at a meeting which lasted nearly five hours brings forward a statement, which bears as much relation to a profit and loss account of the trans- action as that the well-known sum of 2 and 2 makes 10.

Canon Wood acknowledged that of the increase of the rates from 51 to 91a decrease in the rate- able value accounted for one penny. The financial statement a'; the meeting of the School Board in November shows that another penny is swallowed up in the balance at the bank. Outside these fac- tors Mr Cunningham's faulty figures show a further reduction, Where are the ratepayers going to be landed on this question ? If Mr Cunningham and his colleagues had faith in the figures presented. Why did not they use their majority to have them entered on the minutes? Was it lack of courage ? The decrease of Ihe rateable value and the bank balance explains 21 of the: increase and Mr Norman's task in showing that the figures of Mr Cunningham are not all they seem would appear to be easy. It is certain the question will not be left where it was on Monday night. Mr Cuuningham's blessing not- withstanding. For the Progressives to allow School Board education to be saddled with expenses it ought not to bear would be unpardonable in the extreme, and there can be no doubt that Mr Nor- man, backed by the infl isnce ofO Julie opinion as shown by his commanding position on the poll, will return to the attack.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

With Houghton away, and the threequarter line weakened by Wilkinson taking his place, and Richardson on the sick list, the expected happened at Broughton,by the Rangers winning by six points to two. This result, however, was not attained without a severe struggle. observe that the Man- ches'er critics again attacked Runcorn for an alleged propensity to the kick and rush style of play. Now we all know that the wearers of the green have their faults, but much of the blame which is sought to be attached to Runcorn for deterioration in play is both unde- served and unjustified. A certain football scribe of eminence three months ago made an attack on the team in a manner that no circum- stances would warrant and others, jackal-like have since taken up the cry. I am too impartial to assert that the team play as attractive a game as they did two or three years ago. At times the men do indulge in too much kicking, Jolley being the leader and the greatest sinner. I have known both Jolley, Warder, and Butterworth kick where passing would have had better results. I have seen the men this season execute passing move- ments that could not be excelled. .A judicious blend of kicking and vigorous following up and quick passing movements tend to bewilder the enemy and win matches. I have seen clubs on Runcorn ground this season who placed Runcorn a bid second for uninteresting kick and rush style of play and I claim that Ran- corn is no worse, nav, not so bad as some clubs in the Northern League that I could name were it necessary. What is puzzling to the impartial observer is to explain why is this dead set made 'against Runcorn this season. The club seems to be singled out with malice prepense. Since the Northern Union commenced Runcorn has twice won the championship and always been in the first half- dozen on the league list, and these honours have 'not been gained by luck but sheer merit, When Runcorn get back Jack Faulkner they wdi have a back division second to none for football skill either in passing, catching, fiel ling. aye and kick ing when occassion requires it and I hope to se the team ere the curtain descends on April 30th show their detractors that Runcorn now as ever breeds footballers of the highest class.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovaltst."

Warrington's reputation for being erratic will soon want a lot of beating. On Wednesday last week they ' went down badly before Bradford at Warrington after having beaten the same team at Park Avenue. On the Saturday they journeyed to Hull, to play the runners- up of the Northern League, with no fewer than six regular first team men absent—and they won by 15 points to 7 points. What sort of form can one call this? To be consistent now Warrington should lose points against Halifax at home to-day but I sincerely hope they won't. However the team deserves nothing but praise for the excellent performance at lull, which had nothing in the nature of a fluke about it, &but was actomplished by sheer determination.

One of the players telli me that the team never wen away more confident of winning though so many reserves had to b 3 brought in to fill the vacancies seed by injury and neglect of the working clause. They were all triers last Saturday, and the advantage was at once seen of having men playing for their places in the first fifteen. A smile of derision went round the enclosure at Warrington on Saturday, when it was learnt what sort of a team had gone to Hull, and the halftime score was awaited with unhappy' anticipations. When it came-2 points to nil—hopes were raised once I more, but the final took a lot of crediting nevertheless. It is not like Warrington to put on fit teen points in the second half, and if they would only do it at IVildersp ol occasionally their supporters would be well pleased. Some of Warrington's best games have certainly been played away from home this season—as witness the defeats of Hull, Bradford, Oldham and Runcorn.

The game at Hull was excellently well contested from start to finish. Warrington begun with the .wind against them and by dint of good defensive play they crossed over only two points in arrear. Taylor, the Hull custodian, was unable to resume after half-time owing to a broken thumb, so that Warrington were given a golden opportunity to distinguish themselves. And they took it. Operations were soon carried into the Hull quarter and Harry Foster, the old "A " team threequarter, rushed over from his new position at half back, Fish placing a goal. Very soon after Fish ran in himself and kicked another goal. Then Hull had a turn and got five points—the try being apparently from a forward pass—but Warrington kept the upper hand, ' Fish converting a try by Edmondson before the close, when Hull were well beaten at all points.

No doubt the loss of Taylor weakened the defence very materially, but even the • Hull people admit that Warrington wouldlhave won in any case. They played a keener and cleverer game than the homesters, who have quite collapsed since Broughton Rangers settled their pretensions to the championship by inflicting the first defeat on the Boulevard ground. That the best team won is a true and fair commentary on the match.

Warrington's substitutes did yeoman service. Ratcliffe at full back showed considerable improvement and ran, fielded and kicked with a safety and judgment which earned him high praise. At centre Jones played his best game this season, and showed that he can bold his own if he wants in the three-quarter line. The lecture on trying which was administered to him appears to have done good. Dickenson went over to Fish's side, and the

County left centre and wing had a profitable practice together. Harris shone most on the defence. The surprise of the day was Foster's display at half back. He always was a desperate sort of footballer, and there was no holding him on Saturday, the Hull halves fail- ing often to tackle him effectually. He scored his try by sheer strength and dash. There is no doubt he rose to the occasion finely, and if he had only passed judiciously at times the score would have been larger. The forwards also did well, and the value of an occa- sional change in this department was emphasised by the keenness shown.
About 100 people accompanied the team to Hull and to say they were delighted with their trip does not half express their feelings. They came back much happier than they went.
The Northern League table up-to-date is as follows• _For Against.

P WLD T PTS T I PTS. Broughtonßangers 12 ...16 1 1...35 51-223...15 13— 69...33 Hull •S win ton Runcorn *Warrington Oldham *Salford Bradford l6 ... 8 8 0...19 32-134...17 28-118...16 *Hunslet Huddersfield Leigh Halifax l5 . 5 8 7...16 16— 80...21 28-126...12 Batley Brighouse Bangers 16 ... 1 14 1-1.3 8— 50...34 45-203 3 *Salford, Swinton, Warrington, and Hunslet have each bad two points deducted for breach of the rules.

It will be seen that Warrington, but for hiving had two point deducted, would be second in the list. They have play 7d and won as many matches a§ Hull and possess a superior point average. Several clubs are in the running for second place,Warrington's chance being nearly as good as any, and it would be a good perform- ance were they to finish the season second only to Broughton Rangers. Let us see what they can do by trying. To make a charge for witnessing the "A " team match with Werneth last Satufday was really robbing the public. A more miserable game was surely never witnessed at Wilderspool. The visitors only brought twelve men and yet at the end of the scramble Warrington were only leading by 5 points .to 2 points. The new men, Casey, Bowden and Midge did not create a great impression. The two latter were keen and may develop, but Casey seems fitted for nothing but the scrimm gcl. He and Aldred may be of service I there. Both are well-built fellows. Purslow is another promising forward, with youth and weight on his side.

There was some important business at' the Northern Union and Northern League meetings on Tuesday even- ing, when two clubs were fined for breach of the pro- fe,ssional laws, and having been found guilty, will accordingly lose two points. These two unfortunates are Runcorn and Swinton, the latter club having pro- viously suffered, and there is,consequently, much heart- burning in the respective camps of the Blues and the Greens. We in Warrington can sympathise but no more, for, after all, other clubs' misfortunes are our gain, and there is selfishness in league football as well as anywhere else. The points will be deducted at the next Northern League meeting in February. Swinton will then have a star all to themselves.

Fletcher Russell's have at last gone to the wall, and were,on Tuesday struck out of the Lancashire Competi- tion. Bad management and want of amity with the Warrington Club seems to have been the cause. The Engineers have played some good games and had somo , promising players, the pick of whom in Brown (full- back),Clare (wing), :Jolley and Potter (forwards) have signed on for Warrington. They are down for a trial with the " A "team at Rochdale to-day.

Warrington have a stiff gains with Halifax down for decision at Wilderspool. Fish and Dickenson are both chosen to play for Lancashire against Cumberland, and ‘Varrington's scoring power is thus considerably lessened. Still lam hoping that they will rise to the occasion and avenge the defeat sustained at Hanson- lane on November 23rd. Warrington were the better side on that occasion but they did not get the points. The Halifax men are very smart forward, and full back, the holder of the latter pmition, Little, being a custodian worth seeing.
Isherwood seems unfortunate in his aspiration for county honours, but I hope they will yet come. A more deserrinz or reliable centre than the Warrington skipper does not play under N.U. rules

Warrington's selected fifteen is ; Hallam, full back ; Hockenhall, Isherwood, Jones and Harris, three- quarters ; Burgess and Allen, half backs ; Boardman, Taylor, Morrison, Edmondson, J Swift, W Swift, Foster and Jolley, forwards. Of these Hallam. Isher- wood and Burgess are doubtful, but it is hoped they will be fit. Foster gets his reward for a crbood display last Saturday by being included among the forwards to-day, His dash mayset a good example.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

King Edward the Seventh has taken a prominent part in the campaign against Tuberculosis from its very commencement, and one remembers well the interest and anxiety with which his Royal and deeply-lamented .nother watched the fortunes of the Hospital for Consumptives at Ventnor. An enormous impetus has been given to the movement by the .£200,000 placed at his Majesty's disposal by a gentleman who prefers to conceal his identity, which sum is to be devoted to the establishment of a sanatorium for the use, chiefly, of consumptive persons who are neither rich nor extremely poor, but who are situated financially between the two. The money was given with a view to its being ap- plied to a charitable or utilitarian purpose, and the decision of his Majesty to devote it to the further- ance of the object mentioned met with universal ' approval. For it has been long recognised that there must be a vast number of very deserving per- sons of modest means who cannot pal highly for the kind of treatment needed, and to whom the portals of essentially charitable institutions have hitherto been closed. That the sanatorium which will spring from this munificent benefaction will be one of the best of its kind in Eagland is certain, and that its usefulness as a means of swing life will be widesnread is equally so. The liAig's idea and scheme should bring Ito their aid the best intellects and the fruits of the moat desirable and prolonged experience.

" Mahon " the Welsh Bard, known in the House of Commons as Mr W Abraham, member for the Rhondda division of GlamOrganihire, does not appear to have been greatly alarmed by the evidences he observed during his recent American ' tour, of serious competition between that country 1 and this, at any rate so far as mining interests are concerned. He appears to have seen much of the industrial life of America while there,and reminded a meeting of his constituents the other evening that across the Atlantic many miners work ten hours a day, though they Cease work for an hour at mid-day and speud another in preparing and leaving off their task, and this time appears to be included in the hours mentioned. He does not con- sider the conditions of labour in the states superior to what they are in Great Britain. although he I knows young men who have gone thither and would not dream of returning to the old country. Some of us have had experience of such young fellows when on a short visit to this country, and were not at all sorry to know they had gone back., It is needless to question what " Mahon " says about competition with South Wales. Newspaper readers know sufficiently well that the Americans are not only very pushful, but that they have cer- tainly succeeded in ousting British trade from cer- tain markets abroad. 1

The provinces are once more contributing their quota of Imperial Yeomanry for active service in South Africa. The northern counties figure well in the military records of a notable period ; and the task of selecting the Yeomen of late has been by no means a sinecure. Only the most eligible of re- cruits are accepted, and the tests through which the candidates have to pass are the reverse of for- mal. Those who have not been chosen, however, through some trifling physical defect, are none the less worthy of praise for the quality of their patriot- ism. Some critics are fond of asserting that the wave of patriotism has abated under pressure of the:tedious campaign, and the occa.sionally discon- carting incidents, by which it has recently been punctuated. In the provinces, at any rate, there nas been no sign of this fliccidity. If there be any abatement at all, it is probably no more than sporadic; but one is much inclined to question its existence even in that form.

There is to be an Eclipse of the Moon in April. " What of that ? " will ask the irreverent. Raphael, Orion, and Zadkiel, three famous seers in the esti- mation of a •cvast .number of our countrymen and women, think there is very much in the event. " The eclipse in April,' I says one, " will pro-lace a great deal of restlessness in the country." Why, this deponent sayeth not. But there generally is restlessness just about Ester, and this year we are asked to believe that the Cause will not be the holidays, but the 'clipse. Another of the prophets, however, has lived at the matter in a stronger light, and fore- dila that the eclipse of the moon brings danger of For an °ll!,brealr of hostilities. He is quite an alarmist, readers by this time are weary of war, and if the prowl et: or our wretched Government, no matter which, is because there is going to have another war just an eclipse of the moon, it will be the last straw. There must be a change, either of the Almanac or the Government very soon, or it will be more then the country can bear. Indeed, the people may think proper to revolt against the arrogant Jingoism. that will not even let the moon i have an eclipse fit wants to. It is impossible to discover what British interests are involved. But eor explanation since the tal eclipse of the moon ; tt hh rnd tphreorpehme prophet ys abye s atnhoet ht means a wedding in our Royal family I This is de- cidedly better ; but how the eclipse of the moon can lying the wedding about or whether it foretells the eclipse of a honeymoon, are matters of faith which, it must be presumed, do not belong to the laity. When prophets disagree, however, they do indeed perplex:
Provincial Cricketers and Footballers have especial reason to take exception to Mr Rudyard

I, Kipling s allusion in his latest extravagance, the " Islander," to " the flannelled fools at the wicket and muddied oafs at the goal," since it hits them all in a very tender part. It is hoped by some other writers, to whom Kipling is still the petted favour- ite, that his jeers and jibes and sneers at his fellow- countrymen,may have done a service to the Empire by this poem in the " Times," if only he can stir the islanders to a sense of their shortcomings and the necessities of our Imperial position. Be this las it may—and many of us are notfat all pleased to find our Saturday and Monday's gip era more than half given up to football and crideet—Mr Kipling must have a bad quarter of an hour when he reaches the Cape and opens his English newspapers For the whole civilised world interested in the two national pastimes in question has joined in the onslaught upon that deplorable and never-to-be- forgiven line already mentioned. Even among Mr Kipliug's faithful adherents, of whom the " Times " would appear to be one, there are those who hold that the poem belongs to the category of things that might have been batter expressed in a po.:eibly less offensive way.

except in the Service papers—persistently over- looked. Yet no branch of the army, whether Regular or Irregular, has performed better service or has done its hard work more efficiently and uncomplainingly than the Militia. Thirty regi- ments of the old constitutional force have one battalion serving in South Africa and not a single unit exists which has not been embodied at least once during the war for service either in home garrisons or on foreign stations. The force is, therefore, in a very high state of efficiency, ready for almost any work, and its officers have the advantage of sound training in the actual theatre of war. The question which is agitating military inea at the present moment is whether the War Office intends to take advantage of the condition of the force to make the improve- ment permanent, or to allow it as soon as the war is over to slip back again into the discredited position from which its great services, voluntarily performed, and without the allurements neld out to Volunteers,have rescued it. During the war the Regular battalions have found themselves able to replenish their depleted commissioned ranks by absorbing Militia officers; and thus the force has been what it should be, a valuable feeder to the Itlgular army. The surest protection from con- scription which the country could have is the maintenance at a proper state of efficiency of its Auxiliary forces, of which the Militia has been proved by far the most useful for all purposes.

It may be some consolation, to those who will be unable to visit London to see any portion of the Coronation festivities, that these important events are to be cinematographed as never pro- cessions or ceremonies of any kind were cinemato- graphed before. "Living pictures" showing the great Jubilee procession through London achieved a great success, and were greeted everywhere with enthusiasm ; but. we are told that there will be no more comparison between the pictures to be pro• duced next June and those old views of the Jubilee than there might be between the work of the most artistic photographer of the day and the ancient products of the daguerreotyper. The process has in these few years reached a high state of perfec- tion, and nothing will be spared, we are told to bring before residents in the provinces a vivid representation of the stately events to be enacted in the metropolis. And there is to be no mistake about it. There is to be no suspicion this time of "faking," as with certain views of South-African warfare, the engagements in which are more than probably :fought outilby little armies of the theatrical super kind on the convenient slopes of the Kent hills. The apparatus is already put up, and has been tested to dome extent on the strange and always interesting panorama of London streets ; and there is every reason to believe that, whatever the climatic conditions of the day— short of absolute fog—a great success will be achieved. It is to be hoped, for the pleasure of hundreds of thousands, that this will prove the case; and if the promoters of the scheme make a considerable profit out of the venture, who shall grudge them their reward?

Mr W Gittens presided at the organ. The collec- tions, which were satisfactory, were in aid of the Society Fund. STEAMSHIP REPAIRING-. AT RUNCORN.

When the Ship Canal was made there were re- quiems for the departure of ship building in Run. corn. Ship building may have departed but at the Old Quay engineering works, there is constant ' employment found in the work of ship repairing. Steamships and sailing ships are dealt with there continually and employment found for many artificers. At the present time one of the largest, if not absolutely the largest steamship, ever berthed at the works is underp.oing a thorough overhaul- ing. This is the e.s. Hare,belonging to the Dublin Manchester Steamship Co. This ship has a registered tonnage of 334 tons and a gross ton- nage of 893 tons and has splendid accom- modation for 75 passengers. Once a week the ship makes the passage to and from Dublin and Manchester and she carries each time general goods and cattle. In summer time the passengers are numerous. The captain is Mr Alex- ander Carmichael, a capable and pleasant officer, who has been in charge of the ship for two years. The Hare is undergoing a thorough overhauling,and it is orobahle she will be at Rancorn for another fortnight. The incident is a somewhat unique, one in the shipping trade of Runcorn. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
EARLESTOWN.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT]

Dr Latham cannot by any means be dubbed the silent member of the District Council. He had a fairly good innings on Monday and unless Mr Gil- mour is vary careful he is doomed to lose the proud position he has occupied for so long a time, as the garrulous member. At times these two useful members am o at cross purposes and at others they join bands in a common cause. On Monday they were at one over the nuisance on the canal bank near Newton Common. For years this nuisance of unloading manure from boats on to the canal bank has existed, and as it is close to numerous dwellings, the doctor is doing a public duty in bringing the question farward.:Mr Gilmour resides on the hill overlooking the canal, and be of course, is affected in a direct manner by the question. The Council were evidently in accordance Nvit,l3 the doctor's complaint, as they decided to give notice to abate the nuisance.

From the proceedings of the Council it would appear that we are to have a town fire engine and fire brigade,and that an application is to be mace to the Local Government Baud for permission to borrow „CLOW for fire brigade purposes. The town and district is growing rapidly, and ia the event of a big fire we have to depend upon the services of private brigades. But the question arises if we get an engine and brigade can we be certain if an out- break should occur,that we should have a sufficient supply of water to cope with the fire. It is a step in the right direction to get all the necessary appli- I amass, and p3rhaps the question of water supply will be put on an assured basis in course of time.

Dr Latham's argument that a "Football club " was 'a charity organisation, was a most ingenions one. According to his idea a cricket club, a tennis nib, a bowling club, an athletic association, and any kind of organisation devised for the plessure of its members, is a charity organisatidn, it it is designed to add to the physical development of the human frame. 1 fancy many of the clubs in the district would ba very greatly insulted if they' were told that they wore objects of charity. Of course the doctor was clntending for an object,and to attain his end it was necessary no doubt to stretch a point. In connection with the fo3tball club, I should like to know where its charitable object begins. It is well known that professional clubs are run for the financial benefit of the players and the amusement of the public, not to say any- thing of a yearly dividend to the shareholders, but Of course the dividend question only applies to the first class clubs. It takes a club such as Earles- town all its time to make ends meet, but it cannot by any stretch of imagination he considered an object of charity. lam rather afraid it is an organisation which would come within the saving clause " private profit," seeing the players get all the benefits. I think the football club should pay for the Town Hall the same as any other body of ratepayers not a charitable organisation.
FOOTBALL.

Wigan United 6, Earlestown, nil. Pbew ! What a licking, After rubbing it into St. Helens Town to the tune of three goals to one, the local suppor- ters naturally expected that Earlestown would at least make a decent show against the United, and consternation reigned in the camp when the result became known. There must have been a screw loose somewhere. It is pretty evident that Earles- town away and Earlestown at home are two entirely different lots. What makes the defeat all the harder to explain is the fact that the United were by no means strongly represented. It's no use try- ing to explain away the defeat. The same team ran round Warrington, Ilaydock, and St. Helens on the Mesnes, and the first time they are out of sight of the Railway they go down by six goals to one. Talk about the uncertainty of football. Here's a fine example for the critic.. To—morrow St. Helens Town again visit the Ntesnes ground, and no doubt we shall see the locals in tip-top form again.
With respect to the IVigan match, the Secretary of the Earles3wn F.C. explains that the heavy defeat was due to several of the team complaining of feeling ill before going on the field. Whitehoase
failed to put in an appearance until close on tte interval whilst Leigh played through the game with a bad toot.

Newton are in a bad way at present. On Satur- day they had to play second fiddle to White Star Wanderers and once more before their own sup- porters. The game was remarkably fast and excit- ing throughout considering the muddy state of the ground. Newton played two new men and they shaped very well. The first half was very evenly contested both .goals undergoing severe pressure and bath having their share of miraculous escapes. On one occasion the Star got in front of Horrocks a a tine centre from Kelly , rolled about a couple orysards in front of the posts across the goal-mouth,two of the forwards slipping and allowing the ball to roll harmlessly outside. At the interval the score sheet was blank. Shortly after the resumption the Star g -it in front—a few minutes later they increased tneir lead. Newton livened up after this and a centre from Hill enabled Butler to reduce the visitors lead. The concluding stages of the game were fiercely contested but nothing further was scored, the whistle blowing with the score 2 to 1 in the Star's favour.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A DISHONEST 'BUS CONDUCTOR.—THE DUTY OF THE PUBLIC, At the Warrington Po ice Court on Wednesday, before Mr Birdsall (in the chair), Aldermen Hutchinson and Monks. and Mr Geddes, a youth named john Jones, residing at 9 Barry-street, Latchford. was charged with having stolen from a 'bus collecting box on luesday evening, the sum of one shilling and a halfpenny, the money of Mr Edward Connor, cab and 'bus proprietor, Sankey-street. Defendant pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said the boy was be- tween fifteen and sixteen years of age, and had been em- ployed by Mr Connor as a 'bus conductor on the Latchford route. He was not employed as a regular conductor, but as an occasional supply conductor. Formerly he was employed regularly, but left te go to another situation. On Saturday Mr Joseph Healey. the ch‘cker. cautioned him as to some irregularity which bad been reported with respect to the taking of the fares. That misdemeanour, however, was overlooked. The previens day other complaints were made with the result that the young man w a watched by the checker. Mr Healey went round to the Latch- ford end of the route and concealed himself in a garden which overlooked tke terminus. Be saw the youth, who thought himself alone, turn the box upside down and extract cash from it. A wad of paper had been put into the slot so as to prevent the cash passing into the body of the box. This was a very simple and ingenious way o getting the money. H. aley went to the youth and found in his possesaion the sum of Is Old. which he admitted having purloined from the box. Mr. Connor had suffered a great deal from this kind of thing and deg, ed him (the Chief Constable) to say that as he had pardoned a great many boys and given them chance after chance, he felt it now his duty to prosecute and also ask for a smart penalty. He would like to ask the magistrates to express an opinion as to certain members of the public who really put tempta- tion in the way of these boys by giving them the money, and even told the boys not to put the mOner in the box as Mr. Connor had plenty of moner.—The Chairman said the Bench had-decide.d to fine the defendant 20s. The suggestion on the part of anyone that the conductors should not put the money into the box and even the Riving of money to them was very wrong. The public were bound to put th 3 money nto the box.

BOTH LT FAULT.—Adrian Shirley, 31, Pierpoint-street,was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and child, in consequence of which they had become chargeable to the common funds of the Union —He pleaded (guilty. The evidence 'showed that there were faults on b6th sides. Upon the suggestion'of Mr Shearer the case was adjourned -for a month to give the husband an opportunity of providing another home for his wife and child. IN • San PLIGHT —John Henry Jones, 21, Wakefield- street. was charged with having been drunk in Market Street on Saturday niktit.—A police officer said he found defendant lying drunk across the footpath and bleeding from a wound in the head, evidently the result of a fall. Ile attended to the injury and sent the man home in a cab. His wife refused to take him in. He was brought to the Police Station and Was medically attended.—The Chief Constable said the man was in a very bad way. It was thought at first that he was suffering from concussion of the brain. He was kept at the Police Station until a late hour on Sunday owing to the wife's persistent refusal to take him into his home. In justice to the wife it should be stated that the man appeared to be sodden with drink. He had drunk away whatever senses he might have ever possessed„--Mrs Jones said her husband had Dot been home since Thursday. He then took his clothes away and said he was going to find fresh lodgings. The children were terrified of Mm when he was in drink.—The Chairman said that what had taken place was evidently the result of the man's own folly.—Mrs Jones said she would pay whatever fine was inflicted, but the Chairman advised her to let him go to gaol where he would at all events be kept sober. —lt was stated that defendant had Ge and some coppers upon him, and eventually he was fined 6s including costs. TUESDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hutchinson and Dr 'Fox. SCENE AT A LODGING-HOL'SH.—Mary Ann Browne, 1, Cropper's-brow, was charged with hawing been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street at ten to five on Monday afternoon, also with assaulting Mary Connolly. of I. Crop- per's-brow, and further with having broken two panes of glass, of the value of is 6d, at the lodging-house of William Rogerson, 1, Cropper's-brow. at the Same time.—Mary Connolly. wife of Thomas Connolly, stated that prisoner came into the lodging-house at twenty minutes to five. She was very drunk, and started a bother. She struck wit- ness's husband, and then went out and broke the windows. Her husband went out to prisoner, or she would have done more damage. She afterwards knocked witness down in the street,and a police offi,er came up and took her into custody. Witness had not given any provocation whatever, and had never seen the woman previously.—Prisoner was sent to goal for a month.

A noted bad character named Elizabeth Barker was sent to gaol for fourteen days' hard labour for disorderly conduct in Mersey Street on the evidence of P C Gilpin. ALFEGED THEFT OF CLOTHING.—Henry Caffrey,a stranger. was charged with stealing a cotton shirt and a neckerchief on Saturday. valued at 4. Sd the property of Edward McCann.— Prosecutor's wife, Mary McCann, and PC. Wilding gave formal evidence and the prisoner was re- as.nded until Monday in order that inquiries might be made as to his antecedents.
Manchester Ship Canal.—Proposed Ship- building Yard. _ . .

Important developments are just now in con- templation on the banks of the Manchester Ship Canal at Cad,shead. A well•known firm of ship- builders are in negotiation with a local landowner for a large plot of land situated between the water- way aua Liverpool-road, and if preliminary tests which are about to be undertaken are successful,the site will be adopted for extensive shipbuilding works. A big French engineering firm are also making inquiries as to the price of another field in the same locality as a proposed site for a large iron or steel works. The Ship Canal has already led to to the establishment of other works in the Mem and Cadishead districts, and building operatians are just now proceeding apace in view of further developments.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

At Bold-street Wesleyan °lapel on Sunday, in the morning the pulpit was occupied by tne Rev WC J Neville, whcse aiscourse was listened to with evident interes'. A very impressive United Covenant service was held in the afternoon, there being a good number present. In the evening a large congregation asserntied to hear the Rev. 'l'. Bishop, who took as a special sub- ject " New Departures." He exhorted his listeners to , turn over a new leaf and let past enmities be forgotten.

div.head: Holy Trinity Church.
div.p: Holy Trinity Church.

The choir festival was held in the above Church on Sunday, special music being rendered at both the morn- ing and evening services. In the afternoon a musical service was held, hymns, choruses, and anthems being creditably sung by the choir. solos were rendered in an excellent manner by Messrs George Parr and W Barnes, assisted by Mesdames D.)bsoe and G Floult and Mr F H Randall gave a neatly executed instrumental solo. There were good congregations, the collections being in aid of the choir fund.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Sr. THOMAS'S SCRIPTURE READING UNION.—The annual meeting was held in the Courcb Room on Friday evening the 3rd inst,the Rev Harry V Pigct, MA. .vicar, presiding.—Mrs Pigot attended and distributed the prizes which had been awarded for filling in the texts in the monthly letters on the portion of Scripture read. A delightful programme was rendered, to which the following members contributed :—Miss Miller. solo pianoforte; MissiElAstall, recitation ; Misses Martin and Cooke, dialogue ; Miss Lythgoe, recitation ; Mr Walter Caster, assisted by Masters A Carter, F Hares,E Rogers and T Richmond, recitation and chorus with piano accompaniment. Mr Arthur Down with his usual skid, gave a violin solo, Mr F Rlse accompanying. After a brief statement and report had been made by the super- intendent (Mr J Carter), the Rev Rupert Large, of Ince (Wigan) delivered a very effective and instructive ad dress on " The Bible." The proceedings were closed by the singing of the Doxology.
THE LATE MR. JOHN CHOSFIELD.
Generous Legacy to the Infirmary.

At a meeting of the House Visitors and Finance Committee of the Infirmary held on Friday after- noon. Mr George Dcikin in the chair, a letter was read from Mr T J Ridgway,solicitor to the executors of the rate Mr John Crosfield, intimating that by his will Mr Crosfield had given to the Infirmary and Dispensary a legacy of £l,OOO free of duty. The Hon Treasurer to the Infirmary also begs to acknowledge a donation of £2O from Mrs Beamunt.

div.head: SALVATIONIST'S REMARKABLE EXPERIENCE. Cold Chills, Debility, and Fainting Fits Nearly Ended Her Days.
div.p: A SALVATIONIST'S REMARKABLE EXPERIENCE. Cold Chills, Debility, and Fainting Fits Nearly Ended Her Days.
Marvellous Bile Bean Cure.

"I began to have cold chills which ran through me as if cold water had loen poured over my skin." The speaker. Mrs E Sheldon, of 6, Bright-ltreet, New Brighton, Morley, was telling a reporter toe marvellous rescue trom a serious illnesi by Chas. Yorde's Bile Beans for Biliousness. " It is tour or five years ago," continued Mrs. Shel- don' (now the picture of health) "that I first became ill. I had these cold chills ; and go:, so weak and languid that I could not do my work. My appetite fell off ; and even when I got something tempting to make me eat I had no relish for it. Doctors gave me medi- cine, which, however, did not bring me round. Eventually I got a " recommend " for the Cookridge Hospital, and stayed there under special treatment for three weeks. At the end of that time I was a little I better, but upon my return home I SDOn dritted back into my old state. "'Then, three years ago, I began to hsve fits. I was at the sink one day when I thought there was such a terrible noise outside I could not make it out, so I went to the door. Directly I opened it I was overcome by s death-like sensation. I shouted out, and then I remember no more till I found myself lying down in bed with my friends gathered roun me. Toe " noise
in the str, _ly existed ia my ova head ; and I had fainted immediately I reached the door.

The doctor was fetched, and said it was owing to my age, but another who attended me later said i was colic. rgtlaird described it as: an epileptic fi'. I was very ill in bed for several days ; and suffered in;en9e agony from fiatulence. My body was swollen to a shocking extent ; and when I took food it only made my condition worse. The fits continued and as a rule I bad them every few weeks. They 7nade me a helpless invalid and kept me to my b-d for ten dare at a time.

"A strange thing occurred to me about this time, I lost my memory ;my hearing was also effected, and my sight. I had to wear glasses to thy ai an ordinary needle ; and without them I could not read a paper. I appeared to get worse in general health, losing flesh until I seemed all skin and bone. My nerves became quite shattered, and so afraid was I of being overtaken by • fit that I never dared go outiwithout a bottle of sal volatile, or some Stimulant handy for emergency. I am a member of the Salvation Army, and when I went to the meeting I always. felt more at ease when I . .

had someone for company who knew where to find the stimulant, should I go off in a fit. Early this year I had a slight attack of English Cholera ; and I think that tne consequent weakness brought oa a very bad fit. I was weeks bad after that,and could scarcely remem- ber or see anything. I was in this condition when I heard of a man lac Rothwell—where we used to live— who had benefited by taking Charles Forde's Bile Beans. I was atIXIOU3 to try taem ; and I determined to go in for a course. My condition was too serious for me to observe any decided change at first but I felt sure they would do me good if I persevered. " I followed carefully all the directions, and at the end of ten days I was able to crawl down stairs. I per- severed with the Beans and my strength seemed to come back to me. My appetite also returned, and I was soon able to take many things I dared not touch before. I still went on vittb the medicine until cured. I have now no 'onger the fear of the fits, and I have benefited in every possible war. I have increased in weight, have regained my sight, my memory, and my hearing.. The strange noises in my head, the wind, dizziness, the weakness, and all the other distressing symptoms of my case have, after nese long years, com- pletely given place to health, strength, and renewed vitality. For this I have Chas. Forcle's Bile Beans alone to thank, and I never tire of recommending them to my friends."

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

FIIF,ERAL OF MRS. J. R. JONES.—The remains of the late Mrs J. R. Jones. wife rif the Rev I R Jones vicar of St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, who died under cir- curns:ances already reported in the'' Examiner" were interred in the Sankey cemetery on Monday afternoon in the presence of a large number of sorrowing relatives and fziends. The churchwardens, sidesmen,rnembers of the Bible class, and the choristers walked in procession, the coffin being carried from the brook to the cemetery. The funeral service was impressively conducted by the Rev Wright Willinq, of Farn worth. A hearse was in attendance to carry the numerous wreaths,one of which was placed upon the coffin. The deepest sympathy is expressed on all sides with the sorrowing husband and other 'datives.
