WARRINGTON'S FINK PERFORHANCH AT HULL.

Warringtun took away the weakest team, on paper, last Saturday that has represen ea the club this season—and to do battle against the chosen of Hull. No fewer than six regular first teamers were absent, including Hallam , Isher• wood, Burgess, Morritort, Fell: and Eden. A special train took the team and about 100 spectators at 835 a.m, and bought them back belore midnight. Hull made several changes from the side which has recently been defeated by Runcorn and the taanis lined out as tollows

Hull—H Taylor, back ;Tanner, W Jacques, Townend, and A if ambrecht. three-quarter backs ; D Frank and J Trowell, half backs ; T Stitt. F M liar. Hardaker, F Wade, Bell, Foul- ton, F Spenceley, and R Parkinson, forwards. *Warrington—Radcliffe. back ; Fish, Jones, Dickensian and; Harrison, three-quarter backs ; al en an d Foster, half backs , Boardman, Edmondson, F Swift, J Swift, Cunningham Jolley, Ashton, and Taylor. forwards. Referee. Mr J B Newton, Altrincham. Touch judges, Messrs W Jackson. Humslet. and T G Kilner, Huddersfield. Warrington icued off. and Hull pressed, through a run down touch by Townend. From a scrummage at midway the ball went to Tawnend, who eluded Fish, but was well tackled be Radcliffa Te visitors were then penalised, and Jacques kicked a neat goal. Borne brilliant exchanges were seen, in which nearly all the home backs had a hand, but Frank's final transfer to Hambrecht was adjadged forward. when a spiended opening was presented. Taylor bad his right thumb broken when stopping an ugly rash by the War- rington fotwards. and had to retire permanently. Spenceley was brought out of the rack, and Jacques went full back. At half-time Hull still held a lead o' 2 p Ants to nil. Parkinson resumed, and Warrington sots took up the ettack, but JaNques, with a good run and kick, relieved the prelihure. Warrington payed with great dash, and from a pack at the quarter line Foster scored, and Fish added the goal points. The tackling of the Hull backs fell off conside--- ably, and Fish scored the visitors' seoond try and also added ' the extra points. Frank was to the fore with a clever bit o: play, and raced away towards ths line. Alter m tking a splendid opening he gave at the right mornent to Hamb:e2ht. who scored, but the referee brought the ball back. Hull made a determined effort, and Tanner scored, Jacques con- verting. The absence of a man from the pack began to tell, and Warrington repeatedly gat possession, the Woks gener- ally making headway with toe ball. The tackling of Tanner was feeble, and Edmondson scored towards the close.for Fish to kick the goal. Result :—Warrington, 3 goals and 3 tries (15 po:nts) ; Hull, 2 goals and I try (7 points).

div.head: BROUGHTON RANGER V. RUNCORN.
div.p: BROUGHTON RANGER V. RUNCORN.

The first match between these clubs took place on the Rang-rs ground, and despite the wretched weather there were a great many spectators present. The home side was strongly represented. but on the visitors' side substitutes had to take the places of Houghton,ltichardson,and Farmer. Langley kicked off for Runcorn, and their forwards at once made a very erten lye dribble. which was well stopped by Fielding close to the home line. Then the Rangers' b,seks got going,and Widdeson was pushed into touch by Wilkinson lust in time to stop him from to ;ring. The Rancsers than attacked strongly, but Jolley, ButterwOrth and Wilkinson made several mares ard long kicks, which eventually took the game back to the hangers quarter. Then S games made a splendid opening, and sent the ball to his brAher, who commenced a fine passing movement which ended in Hogg scoring an unimproved try for the Rangera. At half-time the home team led by three points to nothing early in the second hale the Rangers were penalised. and Moulton placed a goal for Runcorn. With only a lead of one point the Rangers played up vigorously, and for the remainder of the game they kept tne Runcorn backs busy tackling. W and S James continually kept their three-quarters going, and both Hogg and widdeson were pusned into touch on the visitors' line, whilst Oram and W James made attempts to plale penalty goals, but without success. Just on ti.e call of time however, Stead scored another try, which W James failed to improve and the result was —Broughton Rangers, two tries (six points) ; Runcorn, one goal (two points). SWINTON v. LEIGH.

This return match woe played Wrd--td;-Swinton ground, in wretched weather, tefore about 5,000 spectators. Owing to an accident in the Oldham match Bob 'Valentine was not able to take his place in the Swinton team, and Leigh were short of Duabavin Leigh won the tans and Swinton com- menced the game against the wind. For some time Leigh attacked, but eventually Dal Bevies, with a fine run, got close to the visitors' line, where he passed* the ball forward to Cooper, and this lost a certain try. Swinton then attacked, and Wallwork dodges over the Leigh line and scored a try fer Swinton. which Preston improved. After this reverse Leigh played up strongly, and had several chanties to score, but, they failed to take advantage of them. By a good for- ward dribble Swinton reached midfield, where if ampson got told of the ball, and etsr a fine run he scored an unim- proved try for Swinton. who led at half-time by eight points to nothing. Wi-,h the win" in their favour in the second half Swinton at once compelled Leigh to defend their line, and Hampson quickly scored another try, Leigh I were unable to tome Swinton back, and after Morgan had I taken an unsuccessful drop at goal Cooper scored another try, which Preston converted. Final score ;—Swinton, two goals and four tries (16 poin'e); Leigh, nothing. HUDDERSFIELD v. HUSIBLET. •

Sutcliffe started this at Huddersfield before about 1.000 spectators. Huddersfield by means of good footwork attacked and Deere dribbled over and scored, Kitchen failing at goal. After the restart Huddersfield still continued to exert pressure until Walter GoNthorpe relieved. Prom a penalty at half way flbert Goldthorpe landed a goal. Scrambling play followed. Half-time score i—Huddersfleld, three points ; Hurislet. two. There was no further 'core bat at the close the referee was mobbed for disailowing a try gained by Kitchen. BRADFORD v. BATLEY. .

This match took ;*lii-c-e.-a-t-Brilf;r-d-17e-fe 2,000 spectators. The home team again played a fine forward game. and in the first half, when operating against the wind, Marsden registered a try. After the interval Bradford adopted an aggressive attitude, and after having made a deid ball they once more reached the Batley line. There was a scramble for possession, and the home team claimed a try, but the referee only allowed a minor. There was good work on the vi store' goal-line, and Broadley tried to force his way over but he was too well held. Then Shackleton made a mark and Fitzgerald took the kick. Bagers got possession and dropped a clever goal. Wilford failed to take the ball and gave the home forwards a clear field, but they were too eager and missed the chAnce. Result :—Bradford, one goal and one try (five points) ; Batley nothing. SALFORD V. OLDHAM.

This match was played at Oldham, before a good number of spectators• Price was unable to play for rsalford, his place being taken by Davies, and on tbe home side Waterhouse played for Spottiswood. Fergusson had two attempts to place goals, but without success, and when "no side at length arrived the result of the game was a pointless draw.

Widnes. who held an unbroken record, made their appear- ance at Craven-street, Hull, in wretched weather on Satur- day. Starks won the toss, and the visitors commenced operations. Barry obtained possession and tvansf erred to Jackson who made a clever run down touch. From the ensuing scrummage Lewis scored from a pass by Barry, but Tulloch failed at goal. Tolloch fall- ing at goal. This match was played at Wigan on Saturday. The posi- tion of the clubs in the League lent additional interest to the match. Grundy scored with a, capital cross shot. Grime having no]chaace. Barlestown played up after this, and Settle skimmed the, bar. rialf-time : Wigan 1 goal, Hatlestown nil. After the interval the United attacked,and a shot by Gerrard was headed away by Leigh. Stansfield, however, met the ball and gave Grime no chance. This early success so encouraged tha home lot that they were soon pressing again. div.head: SIX WIDNES PLAYERS BADLY 11A.ULED
div.p: SIX WIDNES PLAYERS BADLY 11A.ULED

A Widnes pressman interviewed several of the Widnes players after their return from Hull on Saturday, and saw signs of the grave treatment they sustained at the hinds of both opponents and spectators. Almost immediately after their entry into the town at noon, much hostility was shown to them, and even when the game started they were greeted in an uproarious manner. Players were struck during the game. and at the close the team was escorted to the station by a posse of police. Several of the players were subjec!el to violence, even with the protection offered. Chief amongst the injorel are —Tilley, fu'l ba,k, black eye and cut on head; Lynch, two black eyes and cut on nose ; P Hampson, forward, cut on eye; Douglas, half—back,injury to ribs (the two latter were taken to a doitor under police supervision) ; Rigby forward, two teeth knocks) I out and damaged shoulder ; Webster, struck on face leaving the field. Their gime at Widnes gave rise to a deal of comment and It Is supposed that Saturday's Blameful occurrence originated out of the contest at the chemical town. Such scandalous behaviour is only deserving of the strongest con- demnation, arid it is hoped that the matter will be taken speedily in hand by the Northern Union authorities.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION.
Meeting of the General Committee.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Northern Union was held in Manchester on Tuesday evening, Mr J H Houghton presiding. The Swinton Club and B Murphy, one of their players. having been found guilty of bte4ch of Professional Law 2, sub-section 0, the Committee resolved to fine Swinton £5 5s and suspend Murphy up to and Including May 1. Professional Law 2 having been infringed by the Runcorn Club and one of their players, G Messenger, it was decided to impose a fine of £1 is on the offending club, while Messenger received suspension up to February 1 next. The Waft Brow Club was fined ifs 6d for breach of Pro- fessional Law 1, sub-section C. The Committee had before them the case of the Brothers W and S James, who were reported as having gone into partnership in a tobacconist business A resolution was carried to the effect that the two men in question could not be considered as carrying out the working clause in such a manner, and that one of the two players must have other employment by 21st inst. William Chalkley, of Sharlaton Rovers F.C., attended before the committee, asking to be reinstated. He had been suspended twee years ago Inc minection with a disturbance on the ground. Chalkley was reinstated from date. An application was made for a donation from the com- mittee on beh At of the relatives of Frank Charleslon, a player who had been fatally injured. The matter was lett in the hands of Messrs Hutchinson and Sedrnan, with power to make a grant of £25. The rules of the Durham and Northumberland County Union were confirmed. J J Dawson, of Pontypridd, Who has now joined Oldham Club, was reinstated from date,

An application for financial assistance was made by the Tyldesley Shamrocks Club on behalf of the relatives of Tnornas Leather. who was killea by playing football. The matter was left in the hands of Messrs Reddish and Hammersley, with power to make a grant up to £as.

PLAYERS SUSPENDED.

On Wednesday evening, at the Spread Eagle HoLel, Man- chester, the complaint laid by Widnes against Hull Kingston Hovers on the grounds that at the match at Hull on Satur- day last the Widnes players were intimidated and assaulted by the Hovers' supporters was inquired into. The game in question resulted in the first defeat of Widnes in the com- petition, and needlese to say the allegations against the Hovers created much interest. As a result of the delibera- tions, Dabney. of Hall, was suspended pending his appearance, whilst Lynch, Widnes, and Fletcher, of the Rovers, were suspended to the end of March, and it was decided that notices warning spectators of unruly conduct be posted on the Hull Kingston hovers' ground before Saturday next. The alteration ordate of Barrow v Widnes from February 20th to February lith was aonfirrned. The other business was confined to fines for late starts and confirmation of registration of players.

div.head: CURE FOR DEAFNESS IN OLD
div.p: A CURE FOR DEAFNESS IN OLD
AGE

In the reports of the D.ou,t Institute, issued during the last ciaarter of 1901, will be found a surprising number ot cures of Deafness in old age. For the benefit of those interested we find space for a brief account of complete recsyery of bearing after years of Deafness at a very, aavaneed age. This remarkable result is shown in the case of Mrs. J. V. Swan, 75 years old, of Guard- bride, Fife. Her Deafness was caused by Catarrh of the middle ear, and was SO pronounced that the patient could no even hear a clock tick. The cure effected by the Droust treatment is reported as follows:- 13, Macgregor's Buildings, Guardbridge, _ Fife, Dec. 3, 1901.

Dear Sir,—l have great pleasure in testifying to the efficiency of the remedy, that was spoiled in my wife's case, as being a perfect cure of her Thafness. She was so bad that she could hear nothing unless spoken very loud close into her ear, now she hears as well as ever she did.—Yours truly, J. W. SWAN.

Those who desire to obtain further —information re- garding the Drouet Treatm-nt will find a complete des- cription in the " Journal for the Deaf," which is pub- lished each month, with a " Supplement," containing a monthly report of the cures effected by this method. A free cony of the latest issue of tie " Journal for the Deaf," and " Supplement" can be obtained by post on application to the Secretary, Regent's Park-road, London, N. W. Each "Journal " is accompanied by a Patient's Re- port Form,which enables applicants suffering from deaf- ness, or any disease of tht! ears, nose or throat, to re- ceive lull information of the treatment necessary to effect a cure. Any advic6 by correspondence is abso- lutely free, as are also consultations by means of the Report Form.

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this committee was held in the thud Room at the Workhouse on Friday mornin' g Mr G Pilling presided and there was also present: Messrs A J ioUey,WiUiain Houghton,S Davies, J Clarke, A Jolley, J Billings, with J C Sutton (olerk),S Sutton (assistant clerk,')William Owen (valuer) and W H Woodcock (assistant overseer.) THE ASSESSMENT OF THE OLD COFFEE HOUSE.

Mr UNswoaTii, solicitlr, appealed on behalf of Mrs Brown, of the Old C)ffise House, Horsemarket-street, against an assessment of the licensed premises, amount- ing to £lOO gross and £93 nett. The assessment, he said. WAS increased about t welve months ago from £9O gross and £76 10s nett. It was a tied house belonging to Messrs Greene'', Whitley and Wmpany and the rent paid by Mrs Brown was £55 a year. He understood that the house was valued by the commit:ee's valuer in 1894, and he would like to know what the valuation was at that time.

Mr OWEN, on referring to his books,"said his valuation in 1894 was £9O gross and £76 103 nett. Mr UN3WORTH said he would be able to show them that since tio at vdu act 1,1 the noise had no: increased in value. Me;srs Greenall, Whitley and C 3., had furnished him with a statement showing the number of barrels of beer sold during the lass five years, and with regard to the sale of spirits, Mrs Brown had kept a book which was checked by the excise °fillers. 'rne effect of these two statements was that for the year 1900-I—that was the year of the in- creased valuation-26i barrels less wore sold than in the previous year. As a matter of fact the number of barrels sold was considerably less than in any of the previous five years. With regard to spirits, if they 1 compared the sales during the three years of 1896-7-3 ' and contrasted them with the three succeeding years of 1899-1900 and 1901 they would find that 71 gallons less had been sold during the last three years than in the three years previeusly. In the face of that he did not see how anyone who desired to be just could increase the assessment. It had been held in the HGUB9 of Lords that the q lantity of trade done in a tied house was a critarion bound to be considered in the rat- ing of a house. That being so, the figures he had put beim them di I net justify the increase in the assess- ment. On the contrary they clearly showed that the assessment, if anything, ought to have been reduced. In consequence of the a,sessznent ming increased to £llO gross, Mrs Brown had been called upon to pay £5 a year extra for excise duty. Mils Brown was a widow with seven children to support and it took her all her time to make ends meet.

The Clerk pointed out that the fact of the house being a tied house wis an element to be taken ipt3 considera- tion in assessing a !kneed house. In answer to the Clerk,Mr UNswonTu considered that the Old Coffee House was doing a very small!trade in comparison with other houses. There were houses in the vicinity selling ten barrels a week. • Mr A J JOLLEY said the Committee. after a careful revision of the assess .ments of licensed houses, arrived at what was thought an equitable decision. He pro- posed that the Committee make no change. A great deal of i,formation had been given which had only a slight bearing on the point at issue. There were ordinary trade premises paving a substantially higher rent, with considerably less frontage. Mr WILLIAM FIOTJGHTOM seconded the proposition.
An amendment was proposed by Me A JOLLEY, pre, posin to reduce the assessment to £95 gross and £Bl rateable.
Mr S DAV/ES secondeJ,
The amendment was n'arried.

The CLERIC pd,ont that when Mr Browne went through the revised list on behalf of the licensed vic- tuallers, an understanding was came to that no altera— tion should be made in the assessments for the ensuing five years. VAIXER'S REPJRT.

div.head: North Chethire Hunt at Daresbury. _ .
div.p: The North Chethire Hunt at Daresbury. _ .

The North Cheshire Hunt met at Daresbuiy on t aturday, and the field was large, Scent lay badly during the cold wet morning, but later on the weather improved, and there was good and enjoy- able hunting. The borne covers,the Firs and Rose- wood,were tenantless,and then an attack was made upon the Willow Beds. A tricky fox was pushed out, but he dodged backwards and forwards and eventually was lost by Daresbury Firs. A ten minutes' bunt from Newton followed,the fox travel- ling to Owl's Nest and back towards Newton,where the negotiations of some heavy country prcved his salvation. A ring was made from Grimsditoh, the quarry getting to ground by Owl's Nest. Still another fox was forthcoming at Whitley, and after forcing the pace hard by Cobbler's Gorse lac was I killed in the Rhododendrons. Satisfactory sport was obtained from Cobbler's Gorse,a good fox run- ning over the road towaras Arley,then bearing left- handed. He passed through Stratton and Birchall to Bradley Gorse. There was a check at Birchall's but hounds cast over the road and pughed the quarry on further, the fox being victorious after nearly half an hour's hunt.

div.head: AN ASCENT OF MONT
div.p: AN ASCENT OF MONT
BLANC.
Trying Experiences.
[By J. H. Kisby.]

On a very hot day in August, 1901, :accompanied by Mr. J. Martin Wood, of Newport, M0n.,1 drove from St. Gervais to Chamonix. This is a very beautiful drive over very steep gradients, so that the diligences can only go at a walking pace for a long distance. The road on the left bank of the River Arve at first ascends gradually, with the torrent almost immediately below A. Then through an opening in a wooded valley we had a lovely view of the Aiguille du Midi and the Dome du Gunter. The summit of Mont Blanc, however, is hidden. The scenery all the way to Chamonix is extremely picturesque. At last we entered the valley of Chamonix, and the view opened out. The glaciers and giant summits of the Mont Blanc range offer one of the grandest and most remarkable spectacles that it is possible to imagine. We spent a very pleasant week in Chamonix doing some good climbing, including the ascent of the Aiguille de la Floriaz, 9,700 feet. This affords a good introduction to more considerable climbs. During the whole of the time we spent in Chamonix, my friend was slowly but surely working himself up for tackling the ascent of Mont Blanc. I had no particular ambition ' for this as I thought the labour, and not least the ex- pense, would be quite disproportionate to the enjoy- ment we should have in its successful acconiplishment. My friend, however, thought the reverse, and seeing that his tranquillity was so deeply disturbed, I deter- mined to accede to his request to accompany him, at any rate as far as the Grands Mulets. We now arrived at the evening before oar proposed ascent and decided to hold solemn con- ference with the "Guide Chef' on the ways and means. He is the Lord Chamberlain, who licenses and regulates all such performances. Twoyery capable guides were engaged, one of whom, Joseph Couttet, could converse in English, but the youtiger man, Alex- andre;Tairraz, could not understand a word of English and not very much of our long-forgotten French. Our outfit was thoroughly looked to and then we retired to rest. The weather looked somewhat doubtful next morning and the guides were not sure whether the ex- pedition would not have to be postponed. Finally it was decided that we could make a start, so we packed up and I carried a rucksac loaded with extra warm clothing that would be useful on the second day, when we should arrive in the icy solitudes. We set off at 10 a.m., the weather in the meantime having much improved. Meeting tourists on the way our guides informed them with due solemnity that we are en route for the great mountain. We arrived at Pierre'Pointue at 12 o'clock. For the first part of the way the path is through a forest, the remainder is shadowless. The pavilion at the Pierre Pointue, 6723 feet, is a rough building and is kept by the lessee of the Grands Mulets. We had lunch here; prices very high. The view from this point is very fine, embracing most of the valley of Chamonix. The mule path comes to an end at this' place and from the Pierre Pointue to the Pierre d l'Echelle there is a rough path gradually approaching the right bank of the Glacier des Bossons. Here we bid adieu to all vegetation and the path be- comes very stony and steep and lies in a huge gully shutting out all prospect and blazing with heat. The Pierre a l'Echelle takes its name from the habit which was formerly indulged in of carrying a ladder about'to use for crossing crevasses. The ladder,or ladders,were usually left here. From this place the rocks called the Grand Mulets can be seen. We were soon on the ice, a huge waste of purest frozen snow, tending upwards at a moderate e evation and riven in parts by irregular crevices. At the junction '—the point of union of the eastern Glacier de Taconnaz and the Glacier des Bossons the ice is a great deal torn and broken. Huge blocks of ice are piled in all directions and most of the crevasses are from 200 feet to 500 feet deep and of the most enchanting hues, blue in some parts, in others, emerald green. The passage of the glacier generally takes about two hours, but the time varies with the state of the ice. In bad weather this passage, which is scarcely:a mile and a half long, is trying even to experts. Mr. Whymper states there have been occa- sions when it has been impossible to the elite of the guides of Chamonix. After crossing the most crevassed spot where the two ice-streams touch, the route lies up steep slopes which turn from ice to neve at the base of the Grands Mulets. We made the passage without meeting any serious difficulty. Of course we were roped together and exercised much care in the passage of the crevassed portion. We met a party coming from the Grands Mulets ; a young gentle- man roped on to three guides. We arrived at the Grands Mulets at six o'clock ° feeling tired and very cold. While a rough dinner was being prepared we had a short rest and covered ourselves with 'sheepskin rugs. The guides then summoned us to dinner for which I was quite ready as I had not partaken of any food since breakfast. I had some difficulty in rousing my friend to join me at the most awful apology of a meal I ever had. It reminded me keenly of Sancho-Panza and the repast he sat down to while governing the islands. We commenced with flavoured hot water—l mean soup, This was succeeded by a couple of very small cutlets which had been frozen, for how many months I cannot say. The dinner suddenly ended at this point. My friend expostulated, but it was no use, we could have nothing else. We managed, however, to get some mouldy bread toasted and some 'very weak tea, which later our peasant host rendered very slightly forte. We now wrapped up as it was bitterly cold, and went out- side the hut to see the sun set. This was very fine,and we shall never forget the glorious spectacle. The Grands Muletsc 10,113 feet, are a narrow chain of dark granite rocks, which break out of the snow that clothes the exterior of the mountain. This resting place on the ascent of Mont Blanc, was discovered by the earliest explorers of the mountain. It occupies a very commanding position. The hut erected here, like the other one at the Pierre Pointue is the property of the Commune of Chamonik. The prices for food, etc., are as high as the situation. There is no water save that which is melted from snow, and this gave our tea a very disagreeable taste. About 8 o'clock we ' retired to rest and at 12.30 the guides roused us and we made a poor breakfast of sour bread, butter, honey, and very thin tea. We then put on all our extra clothes. I wore a woollen suit, two flannel shirts, arctic cap, thick woollen gaiters reaching above the knees, and thick woollen gloves. We left the Grands Mulets at 1.30, the leading guide having the lantern. ' After leaving the upper end of the rocks, we traversed the Glacier de Taconnaz from one side to the other, then turning to the left we mounted directly towards the summit through valleys of ice, climbed white slippery slopes of snow hardened by the night's frost, and crossed a number of crevasses until we reached the Petit Plateau. I was reminded of Justice Talfourd when he made an attempt to ascend Mont Blanc in the year 1843. He wrote. "When we began to ascend,the snow was found so hard and so steep, that we were obliged to pause every ten spaces while the guides,with hatchets, cut steps. Everyone, I believe, performs some part well ; kat least few are without some gracb or power,whicli they are found to possess in a peculiar de. gree if the proper occasion occurs to rouse it into action; and,l performed the stopping part admirably. While we stood Still I felt as if able to go on; and it is possible that if the progress had always been as difficult, and consequently as slow and' as replete with stoppages, I might eventually have reached the summit, unless first frozen. But unluckily for me these occasions of halting soon ceased ; for the now became so loose, as to pre- sent no obstacle excepting the necessity of sinking to the knees at every step." Day now began to dawn; first a pale light over- spread the eastern sky,which increased,as we ascended, to a daffodil titlge ; higher up the sky was violet, and deepened by degrees into the deep blue of the zenith. The snow had been gradually getting deeper and the ascent much more wearisome. Our way went up a steep incline to the Grand Plateau, our feet sinking deeper in the snow as we ascended. The Grand Plateau is an immense field of snow in the midst of the highest pinnacles of the mountain, it is nearly level and in crossing there is a slight descent. We halted here a few minutes and took some slight refreshment. The guides arranged the four ice-axes - for a seat on the snow. We were much struck with the ghastly appear- ance of our faces ; we were all feeling well, however, and in good spirits. Contrasted with the white spaces above and around us were the dark mountains on the opposite side of the valley of Chamonix, around which masses of cloud were forming. We set off again in a few minutes, turning to the right and reached the depression between the Eome du Godter and the Bosses du Dromadaire, and reached the Cabane des Bosses, 14,327 feet, erected in 1890 by M. Vallot. Here we rested some little time for the weather was assuming a very unfavourable character, and immediately after reaching the Refuge Vallot, we found ourselves in the midst of drifting clouds, which obscured the summit and also the route. We consulted with the guides whether it was possible

n such weather to attain the summit;Couttet suggested that we should return ; this we declined to do unless they wished to do so on their own account. Finally it was decided to go on. We now kept to the crest of the ridge called the Bosses du Dromadaire all the rest of the way to the summit. This is a favourite route at the present day, but was long deemed impossible. In settled weather it presents no particular difficulty, but when the snow on the ridge turns to ice, or when severe wincl or cold is experienced, it is still enough to' test the resources of the most accomplished and deter- mined mountaineer. This route is of surpassing beauty, and there is no more magnificent walk in the Alps than the ascent of Mont Blanc by the Bosses du Dromadaire, and the descent by the Mur de la Cote and the Corri- dor. Unfortunately for us the clouds obscured everything. They dissolved for a moment or two and revealed to us the lovely valley of Chamonix on our left and a glimpse of Italy on our right. Our progress was slow as every step had to be cut and the wind blow- ing from the Italian side chilled us to the bone. None of us suffered much from the unpleasant experiences that many persons do at such elevations ; these are nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness, sometimes with bleeding at the nose, eyes, or ears, and by an utter prostration of strength. It was a great relief to stop occasionally but rather embarrassing as Couttet, the leading guide, urged Me to increase my pace, emphasizing his remarks by a good_ pull on the rope at- tached to my waist. At the same time Wood shouted for me not to go so fast as he was not firm in his steps, at the same time giving me a good ttig backwards. How- ever the end of our long toil was close at hand and in a few minutes we stepped upon the crown of the monarch, with a feeling of gratification that it is im- possible to describe. The height of Mont Blanc is 15,781 feet. I In the winter of 1894-5, thermometers were placed in the interior and on the exterior of the observatory on the summit of Mont Blanc, and it was found that the former registered-31 degrees and the Ilatter 45 degrees below zero of Fahrenheit._

In our case the view from the summit did not repay us for our labour, for as a matter of fact we could only see ourselves and the snow and heavy mist. We just glanced at Dr Janssens observatory on the summit, and Couttet fearing a snow storm which threatened, we unanimously turned for the descent by the same route. Our guides steered us properly through the I thick mist to the Grands Mulets where we arrived at 5 -p.m. ; during the last part of the way the ' snow and hail was falling continuously, proving the correctness of our guides' judgment. We , found the descent very trying, as the snow 3 was now very sac and we sank in it to our knees and occasionally I would disappear to the Waist. Where it was safe we had some long and delightful glissades. I had the honour of discovering the lantern we had left " in the snow in the early morning. Everything had a>',l fantastic and ghostly look. We left the Grands Mulets in bad weather and here I must say I felt very doubt- ful whether our guides could discover a safe passage of the glacier. My fears were not unfounded for in a short time they were both at fault, but owing to their consummate knowledge of the glacier, they traversed first to one side of a difficult place and then another as required. Never was the necessity of good guides shown more than in our second day's experience. Time after time we were landed in such perilous places that it was impossible to proceed and we had to retrace our steps or traverse right or left. Darkness was rapidly coming on and the guides were very excited and rather impatient with us as we amateurs were determined to play the safe game and proceed slowly in places where steps had to be cut. I felt sure it was a case of spending the night on the glacier, but after all I was mistaken, and by a magnificent tour de :Awe our men fought a way through all difficulties, and at last we had passed al the enormous seracs and crevasses. It was 7.30 when we landed on terra firma again and left the ice world behind us. It was quite dark when we reached the Pierre Pointue and found the landlord retired to rest. We halted here and had an enjoyable smoke and passed the glass round to our excellent guides. We left at 9 p.m. in inky darkness and pouring rain, and before we reached the valley Tairraz stumbled and .sprained his ankle. I waited behind the others for him and shouted to him but re- ceived no answer, and though I returned some distance could not find him, and did not see him again until neat morning. Probably he limped home by some short cut through the forest. We arrived at our hotel in 'Chamonix at 10.30, drenched to the skin and exceed- ingly tired. We slept well and next morning felt no ill effects, except the usual stiffness, and our faces were badly burnt. The stiffening of the skin made opening ones mouth to eat,a matter in which all one's ingenuity ' was required, and the blisters with which our faces were covered rendered shaving or washing a misery and for some days we presented a curious appearance. Tairraz lost his snow glasses at the Grands Mulets on the descent, and he suffered considerably the next day or two from the glare of the snow.

The Amateur Dramatic Society's Performances. As the result of the three nights' performances at the Royal Court Theatre the sum of £33 has been banded over by the Secretary (Mr Arthur Browne) to the treasurer of the Infirmary and Dispensary. 1 his is exactly the same sum as was realized last year. Death of Mrs. T. Amos. Our readers will hear with regret ot the death of Mrs. Amos (wife of Mr. T. D. Amos, headmaster of the Practising School, Hamilion-street, and-eldest daucihter of Councillor Smethurst), which took place at her residence, 38, Padgate-lane, on Satur- day afternoon. The deceased lady, who was well- known and highly respected, had been in a delicate state of health for several months, and the cause of death Was heart disease and pneumonia. Her medical attendant was Dr. Langdale. Much , sympathy is felt for Mr. Amos and Mr. Smethurst land family in their bereavement. Funeral of a Volunteer. The remains of the late Private M. Grady, of F Company, of the Ist V.B. South Lancashire Regi- ment, whose death through a fall downstairs was reported in our last issue, were interred with mili- tary honours at the Cemetery on Saturday after- noon at 3.80. An escort, under the command of Captain Appleton' and consisting of the sergeant and 13 rank and file, paraded at headvarters at 2.30 and, with the regimental band, proceeded to the late residence of the deceased, ,wbere a funeral procession was formed and marched to the ceme- tery for the interment of the remains. The firing party were under the direction of Colour•Sergean Cliffe. The deceased was one of the first contin- gent which accompanied Captain Appleton to South Africa, and was a popular member of the battalion.

div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JAN UARY 10 1902 OLD FOLKS TREAT.

of food consumed, which was always of the best, was about half a ton. Many helpers were engaged for weeks prior to the treat in collecting subscriptions and making the requisite arrangements, and he thought it was only fair to them to say that they not only subscribed to the fund, but also paid their own expenses. Notwithstanding the numerous calls made upon those who subscribed to charitable objects—and the: charitable objects were increasing yearly. they had responded so generously to the re- peated appeals of the committee, that in addition to paying their regular expenses they had been able dur- ing severe winters and times of depression in trade to distribute considerable sums to destitute people- In June 1887 in celebration of the Jubilee of her late Majesty's reign, with some pecuniary help granted out of a special fund in the hands of the Corporation, the committee entertained nearly 800 men at the Drill Hall and in June 1897 in celebration of the sixtieth year of her Majesty's reign and the Jubilee of the incorporation of the borougb, with further help given by the Corpora- tion,a similar treat was given to the aged poor,followed by an entertainment. With regard to the finances there was a balance in hand of £47 8s 91 from last year. The committee always endeavoured to keep a sufficient sum in hand if possible to meet the expense of one year's treat or other emergenciealAs they lost some subscribers by death and removal every year they would te very glad of other supporters in order to make up for these losses. This year they had suffered a great loss by the death of Mr Harry Toft, who took a great interest in the work of the institution and the committee passed a vote of condolence with Mrs Toft and family. With regard to that day's treat the number of old men entertained at dinner was about 300 whose ages ranged from BO to 86, and the number of old women provided with tea was about 400 whose ages ranged from 60 to 8?. The num- ber was rather smaller than usual and he thought this was a good indication that trade was later than it had been and that the people were in much loltter eircum- I stances than they were a few years ago. (Applause.)

div.head: ;nteresting Gathering in Parr Hall.
div.p: ;nteresting Gathering in Parr Hall.

It is gratifying to know that amid the joys of the festive season the aged poor of Warrington are not forgotten. Thanks to the exertions of a num- ber of well-known townspeople the Christmas treat to the old folks which is usually held during the first week in the New Year, tigis gained a foremost place in the useful institutions of the town, and it will be the hope of all, that the Treat Committee will be enabled to carry out thtir philan- thropic work for many years to come. This year's treat :was given in the Parr Hall last Thursday, and passed off with even greater success than any of its predecessors. Every provision had been made in order that the old people might thoroughly enjoy themselves, and that they did so was evident to all who had the opportunity of wit- nessing any part of the day's proceedings. The preparations for the event had entailed a great deal of work on the part of . the promoters, but they must have been amply repaid by the marked appre- ciation with which their eff erts were received At noon about three hundred old men sat down to an excellent dinner. It was a motley assembly, embrac- ing the grizzled and weatherbeaten, the lame and infirm. In age the guests ranged from sixty to eighty-six. The fare consisted of roast beef, pork and mutton, vegetables and plum pudding, with beer for those Ida° desired it, and that the repast was keenly enjoyed was apparent from the happy faces of the participators. Quite a large number of ladies and gentlemen gave their services to minister to the wants of the guests. Amongst those present, most of whom rendered assistance in this direction, were Alderman Sutton (president of the treat committee),Councillor Smethurst (vice- president), the Revs E C E Carleton, H R Wild, A Inglis, Father Whittle and Father Wilson, Coun- cillors A J Jolley, A Jolley, Forehasv, Malkin, Rogers, and Sampson, Messrs Roger Parr C.C., Pater Chrimes (treasurer), A Sutton (secretary), T Ash- croft, D Fanshaw, Harrison, Watkins, F Aukland, C Reid, H. Ilolt, G Pilling, J J Neild, G Gill, id Ferguson, Thos Longdin, R Shackleton,T Strettle, Harold Toft, end George Lake. Owing to a slight indisposition the Mayor was unable to be present but was represented by his eon, Mr Roger Parr. After dinner tobacco was handed round and soon most of the men were filling their pipes with the fragrant weed. Several short speeches were now delivered. Alderman Sutton, addressing the men as his dear old friends, said that on behalf of the comminee he would like to express ,how delighted they were to see them all once more to celebrate the advent of the New Year, which they hoped might prove to be a more happy and prosperous one than they ha 4 ever before experieneJci. Since they met in that hall twelve months ago many changes bad taken place not only in this town but throughout the United Kingdom, The speaker pro- ceeded to refer to the melancholy death of our late beloved Queen and said that her reign of nearly sixty four years had been the longest as well as one of the most glorious and progressive in the history of the world. Queen Victoria had been succeeded by her son, calls now ruled over this vast empire under the title of King Edward the Seventh. His Majesty had promised sa far as lay in his pewer to emulate the good .example set by his late noble mother in everything tending to the welfare of his people. He (Alderman Sutton) thought they had had sufficient experience of his Majesty's good qualities and honesty to have full confidence in his power and eincnity.
As it had always been the custom at these

annual dinners 'to drink the health of their Soverign he would ask them to give proof that their loyalty to the throne was in no way abated by drinking the health not only of the King but also of his illustrious aid much boloved Queen Alexandra and the rest of the Royal Family. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm,

Alderman SUTTON said ho Was sorry that their worthy Mayor, Mr J C Parr—(applause)—was unable to be present as he was not very well,but they were honoured with the presence of his son, Mr Rog er Parr, to whose father they were indebted for that splendid hall. (Applause.) It must be very gratifying to Mr Parr to find that the hall was so useful, in fact it was indispens- able for the wants of the town. Before the hall was built they were buffeted about from one place to another and they were with great difficulty able to obtain a room in which to hola the treat. Bat since the hall had ben built they had been able to enjoy their treats and entertainments with perfect comfort. He had much pleasure in asking Mr Roger Parr it he would kindly say a word or two. Mr. R GER PARR, who was accorded an extremely hearty reception, said he wished very much that his father might have been present to hear the kind words spoken about him, and to see the kind way in which they had received nig name. He was sorry to say that hi i father was in the house suffering from a cold, or it would no deubt have done bun good to have come and seen them all assembled there. Mr Parr wished him to say that he was very sorry he could not cm and he wished them all a very happy New Year. (Applause). Hearty cheers were then given for the Mayor and Mayoress. Master T PEMBERTON entortained the company with a " Tinker's song," which he rendered in an admirable manner being dressed in workman's attire. At this stage of the proceedings the Rector (Rev Canon Willis) arrived, having been detained at a meet- ing. In the course of a brief speech he wished all present a very happy new year. They were all getting on in years and he hoped they would not forget that " A hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness." He proceeded to refer to the effects cf a good example. A young man's example, he said, had much effect, but the example of an old man who had gone through life and had experience had a very great effect. Mr P CHRIMES, the treasurer made a statement with regard to the finances. He said there was a balance of about £47 from last year and he thought they would be able to raise suffieient money to carry Ilomerhing for- ward for next year's treat. He referred with appre- ciation to the fact that on New Year's morning he received a donation of £5 fro-n Lady Greenall.
Mr W H IRELAND sang " Mary- of Argyle " in a macnAr which delightei his hearers, Mr W H Payton, Mos. Bac., accompanying..
The proceedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem.
TET:37,716-ERTERTAINMENT FOR TRE AGED WOMEN.

At half-past five in the evening about fur hundred aged women partook of a capital tea, consisting of ham and beef sandwiches, currant and seed bread, mince pies, &e., and ample justice was done to the repast. At seven o'clock the usual entertainment was held, the public being admitted to the galleries at a small charge. A first rate rrograrnme had been arranged, and it was presented in a manner whichlafforded intense pleasure t) the old people. The artistes must have been fully compensated for their efforts by the cordial applause and hearty laughter with which their contributions were received. The major por- tion of the programme was sustained by the Imperial Pierrot troupe, who have by this time gained au ex- collant reputation in the town. It was generally agreed that they have never been heard to better advantage than on Thursday evening and for an amateur troupe their entertainment was exceedingly good. The items by individual members of the troupe included the coon songs " Dinah," by H Davies and "Oh Ebenzer," by D Knight ; the humorous songs "On's enough," by W Watkins, " I burst out laughing,.' by E Summers, and" Up in the world," 137 E Gandy, The Artistes acquitted tbernaelves very creditably,all the items b,ing accompanied by an orchestra under the cooduc!orsaip of Mr Grounds. The orchestra also rendered the march "The Brazilian " iii capital st is Miss Armstrong,who poSsPes a very sweet voice, rff -ctively sang "Ferryman John." and Mr R Grounds save a pleasing rendition of the" Kerry Dance." Mr .1 Emson kept the audience in roars of laughter with his humorous songs " Hey up ! its coming," and "Am I in the way," and Mr E A Sanders scored a great success with a humorous recitation. Master T Pemberton again gave his "Tinker's song " in such a manner as to ea'n a vociferous encore. Tim voices of the Latchford Glee party blended splendidly in the glee " Here's Life and Health to England's King " and the vocalists were cordially applauded. Toe evening's entertainment was brought to a close with the sketch "My Friendly advisers " which created a great deal of mirth. The characters were excellently sustained by the following : —Horatio Brown (a Henpecked Husband), E Summers ; Harry Dare, Percy Vane, Jim Merriman, (Brown's Friends), G F Freeman. W Watkins,J Cobb ; P C Beet (a Member of the Force), A Lowe ; Mrs Brown (Brown's Better flalf),lMis.o A Hoighton •, Mary Ann (a very In- dependent General), Miss May Warren. During an interval Alderman SUTTON who has occupied the position of president for fourteen years delivered a shortlspeech with regard to the history,and objects of the institution and als) gave some particulars in references to their finances and the methods they adopted in order to provide the treat. The exact date of the formation of the inVitalion was not known I owing to the ',xis' of a minute b ok but so far as his memory served him and from co..versations some years ago with Mr William Smith the well-known wire mann- , facturer who was then Presid,it and other old mem- beta of the committee, he shou'.l put slown the date of its establishment as somethin ; like fifty years ago,when the treatiwas given in a sm/.1: room to about a sco,e of old men. From that time ,t'n this not only had the good old English Christmas (Omer been provided for old men, but the treat had been extended to poor women, who were supplied with a substantial tea. 'ibe number of man and women entertained had greatly increased until there was now an average number of 800 to 1,000. iOne year during a period of unusual depression in trade the number reached about 1,100. Do you mean to tell me when a man hunts about for ten minutes until he finds the tongs and pulls my nose with them, that he does'nt know what he is doing ?" AN ATTRACTIVE PROSPECT.—The Cook (answer- ing advertisement for help): "I never wor-ruked in a fiat before." The Maid (also answering advertisement) "Don't you like the idea?" The Cook: "Oh, thry it. They do be tellin' me yez can have fine ould rows wid de janitors." AccoeI3IODATING. Mr. SliMpUrEle : "Wha-- what did your father say when you told him we were engaged to be married?" Miss Beauty: "He was most kind. He said if you would call for him to-morrow with a carriage—l think he said your carriage—he would go with you to look at any double.fronted house you think of buying for me to live in." ENCOURAGING.—" Did I understand you to say that dress you admired so much to.day was a dream?" inquired Mr. Scroogely. " es," answered his wife hopefully. "Well," he pro- ceeded very kindly, "you keep your mind on it when you go to sleep to-night, and maybe you will dream one Of your own." "THAT'S a very clever idea of yours, Miss Nellie." " What is a very clever idea Mr. Dolley ?" " Wearing a big hat at the theatre and exasperating everybody in your rear until the curtain rises, and then relieving their anxiety by taking it off and placing it in your lap." "Yes, I know; it is a good plan. It attracts attention both to my hat and to my hair." SERVANT I "Oh, miss, that Mr. Boren: do be coming here again. There's no use eellin' him y'r not at home, fur he'll just push past me an' say he'll wait till yez do come back." Miss Beauti : "Then for mercy's sake, tell him plainly that I'm engaged. Do it in such a way that he'll not try to stop." Servant: " Yis, mum." Mr. Borem (a minute later): "Is Miss Beauti at home?" Ser- vant : " Yis, sor, but she do be ingaged, an' the felly she's ingaged to do be waitin in the parler fur yea wid a club." " Femme," said the beautiful girl, "George Fitz-Montmorency will call on you to-day." The old gentleman started from his chair and brought his fist down on the table with a violence that indicated greae indignation. "For three years," went on the fair girl, "Mr. Fitz-Montmorency has played forward in his football team." The old gentleman was about to bring his fist down again mad swear, but he paused. "He is the champion boxer of his college," went on the girl, "and he holds the intercollegiate championship for middle. weight wrestling." The old gentleman sank back into his chair. "He will ask for my hand," said the beauteous maiden. "He may have it," re- turned the old gentleman, with what sounded like a sigh,

BLOEMFONTEIN, TUESDAY. Since ,fenuary ht 160 prisoners have been brought into Bloemfontein. All of them have been captured by the columns operating in the Orange River Colony. General Elliott, who is working in the north- east district, captured nine men on the sth, and also discovered and destroyed a Krupp gun.
De •Wet Harrassed.
JOHANNESMIRG, TUESDAY.

De Wet is rerorted to be moving eouth before Elliot, who is following him up the Wilge river. De Wet has little chance of using the captured guns against the blockhouses, as che columns are in close touch with him. The area in which De Wet can now move is becoming very circumscribed.

div.head: 1 ransvaal Boers and Surrender.
div.p: 1 ransvaal Boers and Surrender.
The 15th cf this month is freely mentioned as the -probable date of a general surrender of the Transvaal Boers.
Militia Re-embodied at Warrington.

At Orford Barracks on Monday morning the men of the lith militia battalion, the King's Liverpool Regi- ment, reassembled on re-embodiment. The first con- tingent drawn mainly from Liverpocl, St. Helens and Widnes, numbered 550, and was under the command of Colonel Hand and Captain Edridge. The men left the barracks at half-past two and marched to Bank Quay Station by way of Orford-lane, Tanner's-lane Froghall- lane and Crosfleldestreet, being accompanied by hun- dreds of men, women ,and children. They were headed by the band of the regiment playing appropriate music. The station was crowded azd the men had a very hearty" send off." The men proceeded to Lichfield for ' training, Szo., where they will remain for a short time, afterwards proceeding to South Africa. A second de- tachment of 150 men left later on in the day. The Battalion has an ex-regular—Lieutenant-Colonel W H Hand, formerly of the 37th Foot—in command, and Major the Hon Walter Maxwell as second in command. Captain H K Oram, one of the company cfficers, is at present attached to the sth Manchesters in South Africa, and Second Lieutenant R H opooner—the Lancashire County cricketer—held a commission in the battalion before joining the Manchesters.

div.p: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON

A FOOTBALL LINESMAN M OBBED. On Thursday at Newton-le-Willows Police Court three young Earlestown men, Thomas Lawrence, Joseph Taylor, and John Eaves, were fined 20s and costs, and ordered to pay the advocate's lee for assaulting Bert C Glover, linesman during a War- rington and District League football match between Earlestown Amateurs & Burtonwood onßoxingDay Glover pelted was with stones and mud and struck twice, causing wounds on the face, and he was mobbed, having to take refuge at Earlestown police station.

div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY,

Hope of Barlest-o-w-n- 1.<7,4-e-,-STO-16-14 meeting was held on Monday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Wargrave-road. Bro Cutler C.T presiding. One member was re-instated,and 5 candidates proposed for initiation. Resolved, that the entertainment be postponed a week. Bro Newman read a letter from a Brother inlndia. Bro Roberts also gave his experi- ence in London. Bro Woods read the Digest of No 1 Convention to be held at Wigan, the rest of the evening being passed in a pleasant manner with tales and conundrums. FIRE AT EARLESTOWN%

On Wednesday afternoon a fire broke out in a stores shed in the District Council yard off Cross- lane, Earlestown, which might have bad alarming proportions had it not been dealt with promptly. One of the workmen engaged in the yard noticed smoke issuing from the shed, and at once gave an alarm. A reel was obtained and a good stream of water was poured upon the fire, but the shed was practically gutted before the conflagration was ex- tinguished. All the stores in the shed were des- troyed. It is not known how the fire originated. STRANGE InCIDENT IN AN EARLESTOWN SCHOOL. Shortly before noon on Thursday, an unusual in- cident occurred in the Brunswick Wesleyan Day Schools, Earlestown, when cne of the scholars had a slight stroke. It appears that during the last lesson of the morning, Florrie Patter, aged eleven years, living with her parents in Legh-street, Earlestown, and in the fifth standard, suddenly lost her speech and the use of her left arm. The bead master, Mr Burgess, was called to the class, and seeing her condition, sent her home with one of the teachers. Dr Gauge was called, and examined her. On inquiries being made in the afternoon, it was stated that her speech had partially returned, and that the use of her arm was also returning.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY JANUARY 10, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY JANUARY 10, 1902
NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT
COUNCIL.
The Charges for the Use of the lown Hall.

Mr W Collingwood presided over the monthly meeting of the Newton Urban District Council, which was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. There were also present—Messrs C B F Borroa, J W Emmett, T Ormand, Dr Latham, E T Evans, and J Simpson, with C Cole (clerk), J Bowes (surveyor) and El 0 Timmins (gas and water engineer).

A HAPPY NEW YEAR. At the outset the Chairman wished all present a very happy New Year. "A MATTER OF URGENCY." Before the minutes of the last meeting were confirmed Dr Latham moved the suspension of the Standing Order to enable the Council to resolve itself into the Highways and Sanitary Committee for the purpose of dealing with a matter of urgency effecting the health of some of the inhabitatts—he meant the dumping down of manure at the bottom end of the Common. It bad been going on for two ori three weeks, and was becoming an intolerable nuisance. He hoped the Council woull resolve itself into committee for the purpose of taking action as early as possible. Mr Gilmour seconded and said the depositing of manure was becoming as nuisance to the neighbourhood. He could smell the stench from it at his house. If the people who were continually bringing the manure there were not dealt with they would continue to do so. They as a Council ought to step in and protect the public from the nuisance. Mr Evans supported as the matter was very urgent. The Council decided to consider the matter in com- mittee and a certain course was resolved upon with a a view to abating the nuisance. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

At a meeting of the Technical Instruction Committee, the Clerk having reported the ieceipt of a cheque for £BO 103 by the treasurer to the Council from the County Council, being the first instalment of the grant for Technical Instruction purposes for the Session 1901-2. It was resolved that the Finance Committee be recom- mended to pass a cheque in favour of the Viaduct Institute Technical lestruc.ion Committee for the sum of £BO 103. A letter was read from the Secretary to the Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction Committee, with respect to the circular letter from the Ccunty Council as to the special offer of £2,000 which they had decided to distribute for the encouragement of Techni- cal Instruction in Urban Districts, and stating that the subject had received the careful consideration of the committee, who had decided to spend the sum which may be allocated to this district out ef the special grant as follows ;—(a) In making goon any de- ficiency which may arise in carrying on the Evening Clntinuation Claeses during the current session, which classes have been held since the sksion 1896-97 with very considerable success, and (1) The balance, if any, to be spent in accordance with a scheme to be subsequently submitted to the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council for its approval. It was resolved thtt the Clerk be instructed to send a copy of the letter to the Director of Education 1 for the county. The minutes were confirmed. GAS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this Committee tbe monthly report ' of the Meter Inspectors as to the state of the boiling burners, brass fittings, and tubing was read and it was resolved that the indiarubber tubing for the boiling burners be renewed at the cost of the Council after the same bad been in use for over 13 months if it be then found unfit for, further use, but should the tubing be found damaged after being in use less than 18 months (fair wear and tear excepted), the gas consumer to renew the flame at his or her own cost. A letter was read from Messrs Walton and Co., complaining of the nuisance caused by the gas water issuing from the Gas Works and forming a pool near to their works.—lt was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to inform Messrs Walton and Co. that steps will be taken to remedy the cause of their complaint.—The Clelk fully reported to the Committee with respect to the statement which he had supplied to the Chairman of the Finance Committee at his request, and the Chairman of this Committee as to the financial position of the Gas Depaitment, and recommended that a loan should be obtained to repay the amoutts paid out of revenue. div.head: SUICIDE AT SIXTY-SIX.
div.p: SUICIDE AT SIXTY-SIX.

Sad End of an Old Runcornian. Early on Tuesday morning the Runcorn public were horrified to learn that an old man, afamiliar figure in Runcorn streets, named James Gar- nett, better known as Jam rs flignett, Princess-street, had committed suicide in his bed room by tying his scarf round his neck and suspen ding himself from th bed rail. "Old James," as he was termed by the townsfolk had for some time been in declining health and for years had not followed his em- ployment owing to sheer feebleness. For a long time. when Mr G Hszelhurst was organist, be used ta blow the organ at St. Paul's Chapel, but he had to give up his post owing to a similar reason. Owing to the generosity of a Mr Littler who kept him in board and lodging at the modest sum of 2s 3J per week he was saved the fate of going to the Workhouse. No reason can be ascribed for his act. The inglest was held on Wednesday before Mr R Dobson, coroner. P C Bowyer stated that on going to the house at 10 15 he found the deceased face downwards:between the beds. Tbescarf was tied round the deceased's neck in a running noose and was very tight. The bedrail was about three feet six inches from Us 4 floor. There was a quantity of blood oozing from the lungs. Witness had never known him to have been in depressed spirits though be was a very feeble and decrepit old man. A verdict was returned of suicide while in a state of temporary insanity.

Mr T BIRCHALt seconded the resolution, and said that perhaps be felt the loss they bad sustained more than most present, as the late Mr Crosfield was one of big earliest political comrades. More than 40 years ago they fought side by side, aad a truer man never fought for principle either in that or in any other borough. The Crosfields bad been a splendid family. He could remember three generations. Mr Joseph Crosfield (Mr John Crosfield's father) was then one of the few magis- trates in the borough, and as a boy his (the speaker's) enthusiasm was aroused as he heard his father, one of Mr Crosfield's workmen, speak about " old Joe ": right- ing some wrong, a wrong that needed some strong man to come to the front, and Joseph Crosfield was never I wanting in that respect. Then there was Mr George Crosfield—eot more than a name to soma of them, but a man to whom Warrington owed great things. But for him he believed they would not have had that beailtiful Park in the centre of the town, as be gave thousands of pounds towards the purchase. And he also did his duty to the Liberal party of Warrington. Mr John Crosfield was a downright straight man—a man who always called a spade a spade. He would not have talked about ' • agricultural implements." He sometime gave offence, but he was loved by politics friends as well as by opponents. There was no twisting about with him. He was always there when wanted, and he had rendered yeoman service to the Liberal party. In the 1863 election he (the speaker) had the honour of being co-secretary with Mr Crosfield on Mr Peter Rylands' committee. They fought that elec- tion for five weeks, bolding a meeting every week, and it was very rarely that Mr Crosfield did not speak. Latterly Mr Crosfield's health Lisa not permitted him to take as active a part in Liberalism as he otherwise would have done, but it was not for waat of will, but want of power. It had been said they had lost most of their leaders. There was, however; one thing to be Said, and that was that the rank and file, who were the most important, were with them. It bad been said that The Vienna correspondent of the" Morning Leader'' the war in South Africa bad been a war of rank and file, writes :—The " Tagblatt " states that the name Cbam. and so must theirs be. and they must trust not so M uCh berlsin is becoming a common abusive term in Russia. to men of position. div.head: LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELO. Meeting of The Liberal Association.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELO. Meeting of The Liberal Association.

Pantgyrics from: Alderman Roberts. Coun- cillor Pierpoint, Mr Birchall and Others. There was a large attendance at a special meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Associa- tionlheld at the Liberal Club on Monday evening"to pay a last tribute of respect to our late esteemed President, Mr John Crosfield. J.P., and pass a resolution of condol- ence with the family in their sad bereavement." Alder- man Roberts was voted to the chair, and amongst the large number present were Councillors Pierpoint, Tinnion, Plumpton, and Malkin, Mr Trios. Birchall, Mr William Fornees, Mr J Lengland. Mr Hawthorn, Mr Jeffrey, Mr F Dixon, Mr S Dunbobbin, Mr E V Walker, Mr Willet, Mr J E Warren, Mr John Clayton, (secretary of the association) and where. MR. ZIBA ARMITAGE'S TRIBUTE, The Chairman read letters of apology for absence from Mr Charles Jackson Holmes, Mr Winstanley, and Mr Ziba Arreitams. The latter wrote :—"Newton Bank. Preston Brook. Warrington, sth January, 1002. Dear Mr Clayten,—l greatly regret that I am'preclueled by the stet° of my health from attencling the meeting on Monday evening, and lending my N7OfC3 to the very fitting tribute orrespoct which it is prop lied, to pay to the memery of our late esteemed President. Mr John Crosfield is linked with my earliest associations with the political and municipal life of Warrington, from the time when in the early " sixties " we travelled together to business from Altrincham, and more pertieulasly at and after ehe election in 1868, when I was admitted to the councils of the party. All the old links of that time are vanishing. I can now count from 15 to 30 well- known men who have passed away, who mat regu- larly in the sitting-room nf our friend J G McMinnies, or in that of our friend Peter Rylande. whilat those who remain with us l are few indeed, which is'all the more reason why those who remain should he true and loyel men to uphold the same principle.. in the same unsel- fish way as our departed friends did. I wish to associate myself with any resolution of condolence with Mre Crosfield and her family.--I remain yours truly ZITS& ARMITAGE." The Rev J F Matthews had nese, sent word that he regretted his inability to be reent. ALDERMAN ROBERTS MOVES THE RESOLUTION. The CHAO:WAS said the resolution which had been prepared wee as follows :—" That the members of the ‘Varrington Liberal Association have learnt with the deepest regret of the death of their President. John Crosfiel€l, 'Esq., J.P, and desire to place on record their sense of the irreparable loss which has thereby been suetained. His life-long devotion and unwavering fidelity to the principles of Liberalism, his wisdom as a leader, andlhie kind and generous character have always been an inspiration to those whose pride it was to num- ber thernselvei amongst his co-workers. The cause of Liberalism has lost in him a courageous advocate, and the town a most generous benefactor, and his death come to us all as the less of a beloved friend. We Cl'3;V.' to tender our heartfelt sympathy and condolence with IMrs Crosfield and family in their sad bereavement" Continuing, Alderman Roberts said be wished the reso- lution bad fallen into other hands to move, but,nerhaps, the close intimacy which existed between Mr Crosfield and himself, first of an official character, then of a semi- official and a eoreewhat personal one entitled him to speak with a knowledge and a confidence which cer- tainly had been begotten of the privileges to which he had pest referred. He knew that they were drawn together that night by the feeling that a common sorrow had befallen the whole party, and a further feeling of deep.eincere and general sympathy with the family who had bet such a revered head. Although many of them had been associated during the whole of their nubile life with the name of Mr Crosfield, and although the name of Creefield had always been synonymous with fidelity anOdevotien to the princ'plee of Librralism,yet he was sure they would believe him when he said Chet only a very few could estimat what that devotion had meant and what that fidelity bad "net their friend. He could remember as far back as 1868, when, as a lad, he fol- lowed his father from meeting place to meeting place, alwave, or nearly always, having had the pleasure of listenitne to aemething said by Mr Crosfield, who wae then a comparatively young man. But the same characteristics that remained with him to the eed—en unfearing, out-spoken candour upon every subjmt which Came under his notice in regard to which he felt strongly an utter absence of fear with regard to anything he might say, a strong abhorrence of every- thing that was mean, despicable and contemptible, a splendid chivalry wherever there was a cause that was weak hut which he believed to be right, a tremendous determination to stand by those he thought to be nerve- , cuted—all these characteristics were his in an especial degree at the beginning and were his right to the very end. (Applause.);His sersices were alwayalat the disposal of the party, as well as his counsel and his advice. But there was more than one side to hie character. There were many people who could speak with pere mai know- ledge and appreciation of his private benevolence, his kindly and unestentatioue charity. It would not be difficult to keep them a long time listening to what he (the speaker) knew Mr Crosfield had done in that direction. It was impossible to have a complete record here, but there was a complete and a splendid record in another place of what Mr Crosfield had done for scores of ipeeple about whom the world knew nothing. He could hest express his estimate of that side of hie char- acter by quoting a few words he came across that day : His greeting smile was pledge ani prelude Of generous deeds and kindly words • In his large heart were fair guest chambers Open to sunrise and the birds. (Applause.) As townsmen they had suffered a great loss in matters relating to the material and social pros- perity of all sections of the community. Mr. Crosfield was always a foremost helper, The cause of education had in him one of its most generous supporters in this town, and he was ever ready to take his fair share of Public work. It would be a good thing for the town if those who had:similar opportanitiee,and felt their respon- sibility like he did would join shoulder to shoulder with those who were trying with less influence and less effect to do their duty to take their fair share in the i civic government of the town. If he were to speak to them all night, be could not give adequate views of what he knew to be their sentiments as well as his own. Many of the men that room who like himself had passed the early manhood stage,had been associated with Mr. Crosfield, so long and in so many ways, that they had not folly realized the loss they had sustained to give fitting expression of appreciation of what he had done in years gone by. In concluding he wished to quote a few more lines he had discovered which would, perhaps, give the meeting a better description of Mr. Crosfield than any they could utter:— Lover of peace, vet ever foremost when The need of battling freedom called for men ; Gentle and kindly ever, at distress ' Melted to more than woman's tenderness, Yet firm and steadfast at his duty's post, Like some gray rock from which the waves are tossed, Such was our Friend. Formed on the good old plan, A true and brave, and downright honest man, He blew no trumpet In the market-place. Loathing pretence he did with cheerful will What others talked of weille their hands were atill ; Me daily prayer, far better understood In acts than words, was simply doing goo,. (ApplaustelleThey expressed the deepest sympathy to a family who had lost such a head, but it was some con- solation to them to know that the splendid reputation built up by the Crosfield family in its association with Liberalism was not likely soon to die out. Mr Crosfield, worthy son of a worthy sire,bad left an equally worthy son of a wrathy sire, and he hoped that the success which seemed to be forbidden to Mr John Crosfield in Parliamentary matters might come to the son as some recompense for what the family bad done for the town and for Liberal principles in generations that were
dr3;v^ r
gone. (Applauge.) SPEECH BY MR T. BIRCHALL.

div.p: lIIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above'committee it was resolved that the surveyor be directed to obtain information from tho Sc Helens Corporation with respect to their scheme for sewage treatment, they having decided to apply to the Local Government Bard for sanction to borrow money for carrying out the works. Also that the chairman of the committee be requested to take such steps as he may think necessary as regards the representation of this Council at the Local Government Board Inquiry which will be held at St H.iens. The Surveyor submitted to the Committee his estimate of the expenditure on main roads for the year ending 31st March, 1902 and it was resolved that the Council be recommended to apply to the Lancashire) County Council for the sum of £876 10s for ordinary repair and maintenance, and £452 lie 10d for specia work. The Committee considered the plan (No. 1263 Mission Hall, Vulcan) which ham been referred back to this Committee by the Council at its last meeting for further consideration, whereupon it was resolved that the plan be disapproved. The Surveyor sub- mitted to the Committee his estimate of the coat of vertical steam fire engine,fire brigade appliances, and of the erection of a fire engine house. It was resolved that the Surveyor's estimates be approved, together with the plan of the fire envine house, then submitted, and that the Cruncil be recommended to apply to the Local Government Board for its sanction to the borrow
ther

It was resolved that Mr Henry Ashcroft be re-appointed Inspector of Nuisances for this District for one year from the 24th of January, 1902, with a salary at the rate of £llO pr annum, subject to the sanction of the Local GC% eminent Board, and that a moiety of such salary be claimed out of the County Fund.
