div.head: DR LATHAM AND CHARITABLE INSTITUTIONS. THE ACOODIMODATION AT EARLESTOWN STATION.
div.p: DR LATHAM AND CHARITABLE INSTITUTIONS. THE ACOODIMODATION AT EARLESTOWN STATION.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee it was resolved that the list of charges for the use of the large hall and rooms at the Town Hall be amended as follows :—Concert or lecture in aid of a local charity, to 11 p.m., 103 nett. A letter was read from the general manager of the London and North-Western Railway, in reply to a letter addressed to him by the clerk, of which the following is a copy :—General Manager's °Moe, Euston Station, London, NW., 9th December, 1901. Dear Sire—The secretary has handed to me your letter dated 4th inst, in which you call attrantion to the question of the ac- commodation at the Earlestown Passenger Station. The improvement of the accommodation at this station has been under consideration by the directors of the com- pany, and although there have been difficulties to be overcome with regard to details, yet I think you may take it that as soon as the plans have been matured— which I hope will be very shortly now—no time will be lost in proceeding with the works, yours faithfully, F HARRISON. A letter was read from Messrs Peace and Ellis, calling the attention of the Council to the Clause (Section 94 sub. PET. (1) of the South Lancashire Tram- ways Act of 1900, for the protection of the Joint Councils of Abram, Colborne. *dock, Ince, and New- ton-in-Makerfield. which provides that the Tramways Company shall not commence the construction of any tramways or works in the district of any of the above- named Councils, unless and until not less than £733,000 of the capital of the company shall have been sub- scribed, and not leas than one-fifth of the amount of every share in the capital so subscribed shall have been paid in respect thereof, and stating that the company's solicitors had desired them to ascertain whether the Councils concerned would be prepared to relieve the Tramways Company of the obligation imposed by the Clause above quoted,as the company, do not contemplate

the construction of the entire system of tramways' authoriged by their Acts for some time to come, and for the prAnt, therefore, they will not need to raise the whole of their authorised capital, or even for their pre- sent purposes the sum named in the section referred to. It wa.l resolved that the clerk be directed to inform Messrs Peace and Ellis that having regard to the cir- cumstances under which the amount of subscribed capi- tal was fixed, the Committee cannot see their way to recommend the Council to relieve the Tramways Com- pany from the obligation imposed by Section 94 (sub. sec (1) of the Act of 1900. Dr Latham movad that the minute referring to the prices ta be paid for the use of the Town Hall be referred back to the Committee for further considera- tion. The minute was, he believed, the outcome of a letter that was written to the Clerk asking for a reduc- tion in the price to be paid for the use of the Hall. The reason he moved that it be referred back was that to him it appeared that the minute was of a very indefinite character in this respect—it did not define the word charity. It would therefore give the Clerk an indefinite amount of trouble when people came to engage the hall to the decide what was and what was not a charity. In com- mittee an amendment was moved that the words "not for privAte profit " be used instead of the words " local charity" but of course that amendment was not carried. Charity, the committee evidently thought, began at home, because they said a local charity. Charity, to his mind, was charity all the world over and why it should I be left and conetrued only for local purposes he could not for the life of him understand. There were also different views as to what was and what was not a charitable object. In committee the opinion was ex- pressed that ;rhea it was for the interests of hospitals or institutions of that description it could be construed into a charitable object. He submitted to the Council that other objects could also be construed into charitable objects. There was a large number of people who might be termed the football population. They contended,and he thought!rightly, that they were engaged in a work not only of pleasure, but in the developing of the phys'cal and mental frame of man they were engaged in ras much a charitable work as any other institution, inasmuch as their work enabled men to resist the diseases which hospitals were established to cure. He might go on enumerating other objects but he did not wish to detain the Council too long. Then again, the term concert or lecture was too definite. He supposed that if a meeting were held for the furtherance of any of the objects that could be termed charitable, the promoters would be called upon according to the minute to nay the full price. He thought the Council would be wise in referring the matter back to the committee for further consideration because of its indefiniteness and because of the endless trouble it would give to the Clerk of the Council. Mr Evans seconded.

Mr Gilmour said he must certainly and strongly oppose the amendment. It was stealing a march upon the Council. Be considered that endless trouble would be entailed if they opened the gates as wide as Dr Latham had suggested. He really wanted Dr Latham and Mr Evans to be consistent. They were catering for the public and at the same time destroying their bene- fits and independency. Dr Latham said he did not intend to speak again but he thought one or two remarks of Mr Gilmour entitled him to reply. Mr Gilmour had made a personal attack upon Mr Evans and himself (the speaker) with regard, to their consistency. He could only I say that if Mr Gilmour had only a particle of the idea of what was consistent that Mr Evans andjhimself had, there would be no need for any- one to charge them with inconsistency. It was grossly unfair for any member of the Council to charge another member with inconsistency. He thought the position that he (Dr Latham) took up in the Committee was the position be had advocated that day. There was nothing inconsistent about his action that day. Mr Gilmour's statement was a gross exaggeration, and he could net find language to describe any member who insinuated that any other member was inconsistent. Mr Gilmour said he was perfectly justified in charging Dr Latham with inconsistency, because he advocated evening meetings before be became a member of the Council.but since then he had:advocated afternoon meet- ings Let the public see he was consistent, and then let him go and see" Mr what's hie name at Liverpool." The amendment was then put, but only the proposer and seconder voted for it and the minutes were Con- firmed in their entirety. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee it was resolved that the Council be recommended to apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowinz of the sum of £2,500, to repay to the Council the amounts which had been charged out of revenue since 1897. ITLICATIONS TO THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

On the motion of the D-h-aTinca-n, it was decided to make application to the Llcal Government Board for thOr sanction to the borrowing of the sums mentioned in the minutes of the various committees- The Council also gave their approval to the making of streets as sug- gested by the Highways Committee,and the re-appoint- ment of Mr Henry Ashcroft as the Inspector of Nuisances was confirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE

The Council decided to empower this com—rn—ittee to take proceedings for the recovery of any arrears of con- tributions under Section 9 (1) of the E lunation (Blind and Deaf Children) Act, 1393. SEWAGE DISPOSAL.

A letter was received from the Royal Commission on sewage disposal: stating that they had under considera- tion a question as to methods of sewage disposal, and were of the opinion that to answer it properly they should put under systematic observation for a year or so a certain number of representative examples of the several artificial processes. The Commission had not yet decided as to what places should be selected for observation but two of their officers had visited a large number of works and had submitted a preliminary list in which they bad included the works of the Newten Urban District Council. The Commission inquired as to whether in the event of their selecting the works of the Council for observation they would be willing to comply with certain conditions. The surveyor said the Council should have no diffi- culty in acceding to the request of the Commission, in fact the Council might luok upon it as an honour that the works should have been selected for inspection. Mr Emmett moved that the Council express their willingness to comply with the requests. Mr Gilmour seconded and said that seeing the stinking brook which the sewage ran intowould give the Com- mission greater facility in seeing that their effluent was perfectly pure. De Latham supported but said their effluent was not pure. They did not pretend for one moment to turn out's satisfactory effluent. Be honed tho committee would proceed more quickly with the intended works than they were doing at the present time. If they moved as rapidly with the new sewage system as they were doing at present they would do no good to the Royal Commission or anyone else. •I'he motion was agreed to. LANCASHIRE ASSOCIATION OFaERBAN DISTRICT COUNCILS.

The Clerk read a letter asking the Council to join the above association. Mr Ormand moped that the Council join the Associa- tion, remarking that the obiects were very worthy ones indeed. Mr Bcrron seconded and the motion was carried. This was all the business.

stick to political principles. Theirs was not a party of priviley,e as the Tory party was, a party that was ever- lastingly thinking whether some privileged class could be benefited. True Liberalism went in for the benefit of the whole of the people. (Applause). COUNCILLOR PIERPOINF AND FREEDOI OF SPEECH, Councillor PIERPOINT (who came in after the Chair- man bad spoken) supported, and said he was sure that if there was any man who was able to do proper justice to such a resolution it was Alderman Roberts. (Hear,
hear.) Be (the speaker), was a very minor member of the party—(" N 3, no ")—but having had for a great . . . .
number Of years rather a close connecrilon with it, be could speak not only of the leaders, but of the general members of the party. HO wished he could find appro. . _
priate words to express the admiration he had always felt for the late Mr. John Crosfield. Re was hia ideal of an honest, earnest Radical politician, a. man who did

not altogether at times study his words, but was always anxious to do what good he could for his party, feeling that the good of the party meant the good of the greater number of his neighbours. Mr. Crosfield was a man who always delighted to call a spade a spade, and nothing pleased him better than to have an opponent who could debate with him on similar lines. He was a man of great breadth of thought and kindliness of heart and, to those who knew him, a man of whom they could be justly proud. (Applause.) When he commenced his political career there was a good deal for politicians of the Radical school to fight for, and he was old enough to recollect the time when John and George were fighting for the abolition of the corn laws, and when men marched about Warrington with a small loaf (representing the taxed loaf) on a pikel, and a large loaf behind it—that was to be the result of the abolition oi the corn laws. A great deal of the programme that Mr Crosfield set out to carry out in his lifetime had been carried out, but he was sorry he could not have lived a little longer to give them the benefit of his advice and example in the troublnus times which seemed to be hovering about them. It seemed to him that it was rather an unsafe thing to express what was felt. Even in the great centre of the intellectual Birmingham,prosided over by "My Lord Chamberlain," because a Nonconformist member of the House of Com- mons went there to speak his mind—and every Radical had a right to do so—the arguments of the Union- ist Imperialist party of Birmiogaam were half bricks and any kind of missile they (the people) could get hold of. There was a meeting being held in Bristol that night where the same honourable gentleman—he was referring to Mr Lloyd George—was speaking if the Im- perialist party allowed him to do so. He was sorry their late and revered friend could not be with them and speak of the time when men fought for freedom of thought and obtained it as against these times when they were striving to take away freedom of thought and, he was afraid, personal freedom if they possibly could. In concluding Councillor Pierpoint said that Warrington had lost one of the best of its sons in Mr Crosfield and be hoped the Radical party would take advantage of the noble example he had set. (Applause.) OTHER SPEECHES.

Councillor MALKIN supported and said that as one of the rank and file of the party he had come into very close contact with Mr Crosfield. To work with him was a stimulation and to look upon his face was some- thing to encourage and to infuse enthusiasm into those who came into contact with him. Mr S DUNBOBBIN also supported and said that a more straightforward gentleman than Mr Crosfield he had never met. Mr J WILLETT also spoke and said he well remembered the day when Mr Crosfield engaged him at the works 35 years ago. He could say from that day to the time of his death a better man never stood in a pair of shoes. It had been his (the speaker's) lot on scores of occasions to plead to bim for his fellow men who were in distress and he had never gone away disappointed. The town has lost a good man and the work men had lost a good master. 'I he resolution was carried in silence, all standing. Councillor TINNION, who explained that he had not spoken to the resolution because he had already referred to the late Mr John Crosfield at the meeting of the mem- bers of the Liberal Club, proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Roberts for his services in the chair. He was . .

pleased to see him with them once again. (Applause). During the two years he was Mayor to his (the dpeaker's) mind he did more than was necessary—more than any other Mayor had done in the same direction— in keeping aloof from his political work. Still it did him infinite credit, and he hoped that his present appearance was the prelude to more active work. He hoped the time was not far distant when the whole of the Liberal organization and association would be taken thoroughly in hand. There was work aad scope for them all— (hear, hear, and applause)—and he hoped they would find a common platform on which ' they could work shoulder to shoulder. The death of their friend should be an incentive to them to sink anything and everything that was not for the common good, to start 'afresh, to do his share of the work, and to fall into hie own groove. (Applause), Mr O'BRIEN seconded, and said he thought the greatest testimony to the loss they had sustained in the death of their President that they could give, would be to unite and try to make the Liberal party what he would have liked it to he. The resolution was carried. In responding Alderman ROBERTS said the very essence of Liberalism called for toleration as that was the vitsl principle on which their belief was founded. In con- cluding he hoped the outcome of Lord Rosebery's speech at Chesterfield, after careful consideration and assimilation, might be the re-union of the whole party on lines where some of the give and take would be ex- pected on both sides, and a common platform would be adopted that would ultimately lead the party to victory in the polls of the country. (Applause). The meeting then terminated. REFERENCE AT THE TOWN COUNCIL MEETING. At the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday e vening, the DEPUTY-MAYOR said it wag with sincere regret be moved the following resolution :—"That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of John Crosfiold, Esq, an honorary freeman of the borough, a justice of the peace, and formerly a Mayor of the Borough, and desires to record the great loss which the Borough has sustained by his death, and to express its appreciation of the long and valuable public services rendered by him not only in the Council and as a magistrate,but in connection with many public institutions of the town ; and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to Mrs Crosfield and family the sincere sympathy of the Town Council with them in their great bereavement." That resolution, he knew, was one which needed few words of his to support it, because the man Warrington mourned to•day was a man whose name had been a household word to every one of them. (Hear, hear.) It seemed only yester- day since Mr Crosfield was in fairly vigorous health and taking his share of the town's responsibility, and duties. Warrington has lest in Mr. Crosfield one of the noblest sons of the town and a public benefactor. (Hear, hear.) He wished the spirit which had actuated Mr. Crosfield in believing that it was his duty to take his part in whatever appertained to the management of the affairs cf a town like this was more generally shared by many in a similar position. (Hear, hear,) He (the speaker) had an opportunity last evening of sneaking on the same subject and he should, therefore, content himself on this occasion by saying that the death of Mr. Crosfield had come as the loss of a very old, warm and intimate friend. (Rear, bear.) Alderman SUTTON seconded, end said he had known the deceased gentleman all his life. He was always of a most generous and charitable disposition, and like most honest men, he was particularly noted and es- teemed for his straightforward and fearless conduct in speaking his mind. He was ever ready to take up cud- gels in defence cf any individual or party he considered was being unfairly treated. His loss to the town would be very severe, and they had every reason to regret it. The resolution veal unanimously ca tried.
